speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question of privilege.
The matter giving rise to my claim for privilege arose in the month of December last. On December 18 I rose in the House and gave notice of my intention to raise a matter of privilege. At that time I indicated that the matter might better be raised and discussed at a point in time later. Subsequent to December 18, of course, the House adjourned. It did come back to deal with the gulf war, and this week we have been dealing with the budget.
During that time there have been discussions between a number of parties involved in the events that gave rise to my claim. These discussions have enhanced, in my view, the understanding of the issues among the parties, but the matter has not, unfortunately, been dealt with.
The first thing I have to do here, Mr. Speaker, is to show to you that a prima facie case of privilege exists here, and I want to outline just precisely what that is now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege of tabling today the government's Main Estimates for the 1991-92 year.
The Main Estimates provide a host of details on the way the government will spend most of the $159 billion earmarked for budgetary expenditures, as announced Tuesday by my colleague, the Minister of Finance.
By tabling the Main Estimates, the government is asking Parliament to approve new spending authority totalling $47 billion, while the remaining $110.5 billion is authorized under legislation already approved by Parliament.
The Main Estimates reflected our absolute commitment to expenditure control and keeping a tight rein on the cost of government operations.
Since it came to power in 1984, our government's first priority has been to reduce the cost of government operations while continuing to provide Canadians with the programs and services they need. We made it clear that we were committed to sound management and the judicious administration of tax revenues.
Orderly management of a country's finances requires a strict and continuous review of federal programs and services, and a lasting commitment to spending restraint. In this area, we have achieved major results over the past six years. I will understand if you do not applaud, Mr. Speaker, in view of your duties in this House.
The annual increase in program spending was kept down to an average 3.7 per cent between 1984-85 and 1990-91, well below the rate of inflation.
The annual increase in operating and capital expenditures, including Public Service wages, dropped to an
average 3.3 per cent during the six years our government has been in power. Again, this is well below the annual rate of inflation and far less that the average of 10.4 per cent we saw during the first half of the decade.
The Public Service has become leaner since 1984-85 and is now about the size it was in the middle of the seventies. This happened despite a significant increase in the volume of work involved in programs and services, increased air traffic, a larger number of travellers going through customs and larger numbers of pension cheques being delivered each month.
The heightened efficiency of government operations was the result of more than strict expenditure controls. We also made a point of focussing on better management of the government itself.
Since 1984-85, operations and maintenance expenditures have been controlled very carefully, and departments and agencies have had to absorb any cost increases due to inflation.
Better financial management made substantial saving possible. Measured wage increases have helped to maintain the government's wage bill at a reasonable level.
Altogether these measures have sent a clear message to Canadians that the times when governments were spenders were over. This is particulary important now that we are going through a period of economic recession, marked by unpredictable external pressure that are likely to generate new expenditures.
[English\
Program spending for 1991-1992 will amount to $116 billion. This represents a year over year increase of 6.9 per cent or under 3 per cent after discounting temperate factors such as high unemployment insurance benefits and support to grain producers.
Public confidence in government expenditure control remains a key to restoring the economy to good health. To bolster that confidence and to keep the plan of deficit reduction on track, we will need to reduce program spending further and to take other steps to increase the efficiency of government operations. Tliis requires more than simply a frugal continuation of business as usual. Previous spending cuts and other internal economies have taken the fat out of government operations.
February 28, 1991

The spending cuts we are implementing are bound to have an impact on internal operations and on the level of services that the government provides, but every effort will be made to minimize adverse impacts.
Although departments have not yet determined the precise areas that will be affected, there are some cases where reductions are already known. These range from the elimination of internal government publications, such as Dialogue, to the elimination of direct federal spending on National Crime Prevention Week, to the phasing out of land use planning in the north.
To achieve the savings necessary to sustain a healthy economy and a sound financial position for the government, there will have to be fundamental changes in the way that programs and services are delivered to the public. Departments will have to rationalize their delivery systems and perhaps reduce the number of points of service delivery.
This is a program of expenditure reduction and restraint, and I make no apology for it. We will not ask Canadians to spend more on government than the country can afford.
In the budget the Minister of Finance announced a number of measures intended to bring about both immediate savings and lasting efficiencies in government programs and services. I am announcing today details of some of these measures.

The linchpin of this restraint program is the extension of the expenditure control plan and strict controls on the cost of government operations.
The measures we are introducing this week to control the cost of government operations will generate a savings of nearly $870 million for 1991-92. Over the five-year fiscal planning period ending in 1995-96, cumulative savings will exceed $5.2 billion.
These initiatives will have a direct impact on the Public Service, at all levels. We are introducing a three-year wage restraint program which, depending on the outcome of collective bargaining, may result in the loss of 6,000 jobs. Management levels in departments and agencies will be reduced, and the number of management level employees will drop by 10 per cent.
Routine Proceedings
However, although cost reduction is vital to the well-being of our country at this time, it is not the only reason for these changes.
The measures announced today Mr. Speaker, reflect the realization that we can no longer justify the present complexity and cost of government operations. To serve Canadians well, the government must innovate in the way it provides services and depend on organizations that are managed far more efficiently.
We are convinced that these reductions and reforms are necessary if the government is to have sufficient funds for essential programs and services and if it is to set an example to other employers in this country.
All these measures will substantially change the way the government runs its operations.
There will be a freeze on operations and maintenance expenditures and on capital spending related to existing programs.
To accomplish this, the operating and capital budgets of each department will be reduced by 3 per cent in the Main Estimates. As a result, overall spending on existing programs in 1991-92 will be maintained at 1990-91 levels.
The government is taking other steps to reduce spending on grants and contributions that are not otherwise affected by measures already included in the Expenditure Control Plan.
The Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and Vice-President of the Treasury Board, my colleague, the Hon. Harvie Andre, will review current spending on grants and contributions. This review will ensure that current spending is reduced in line with government priorities and with a minimum of inconvenience to the public. Mr. Andre will submit recommendations on how best to target grants and contributions, promote autonomy and reduce duplication.
These additional measures, Mr. Speaker, will generate savings of $75 million in 1991-92, which will reach $125 million by 1992-93.
As indicated by the Minister of Finance, the government will introduce a bill to limit expenditures. Canadians can be assured that program expenditures management will be done in the context of the fiscal plan.

February 28, 1991
Routine Proceedings

Given the seriousness of our fiscal situation, the government must look carefully at its wage costs. Our approach to collective bargaining must also reflect our commitment to the inflation targets announced by the Minister of Finance.
The government has a responsibility to show national leadership in wage restraint. We are not prepared, therefore, to contemplate wage settlements at greater than 3 per cent annually over the next three years. We believe that this can be accomplished under the current collective bargaining system. We are prepared, however, to introduced legislation if necessary to maintain essential services and to avoid excessive third party wage settlements.
Salary budgets for 1991-1992 will not be adjusted to compensate for new collectively bargained wage increases. There are simply no additional funds available to compensate departmental operating budgets for increased wage settlements.
Any increase in wages must be paid, therefore, through other reductions in the wage and salary budgets, largely through a reduction in Public Service employment. The tradeoff between wages and job losses must be clear and direct and must be understood by all concerned. Each 1 per cent will result in a reduction of about 2,000 jobs so that if agreements are negotiated at 3 per cent the resulting reduction would be in the order of 6,000 jobs.
The choice between wage increases and job losses is not one that is easily made, either by the employer or the bargaining agents, but in the present circumstances of restraint this choice must be faced.
I have already met with the heads of the Public Service unions to seek their support in minimizing job losses. Departments have been asked to identify the job reductions that would be entailed by potential wage increases of up to 3 per cent annually.
Should settlements force a reduction in employment, it is the government's hope that this could be achieved wherever possible through attrition rather than outright lay-offs.

In this time of restrictions, the government feels that senior officials wage increases should not exceed that
which their unionized counterparts obtain through collective bargaining. A certain degree of relativity must also be maintained between managers and the union members under them.
Therefore, the wage increases for members of the Management Category, deputy ministers and heads of Crown corporations will be restricted and will not exceed the average bargained rate of increase for the Public Service.
The number of managers in the Public Service will be cut, as I mentioned earlier, by 10 percent or approximately 475.
This reduction in personnel will be carried out through a government-wide program aimed at bringing down to three the number of management levels under that of deputy minister. It will enable us to rationalize departmental activities, cut costs, speed up the decision-making process and give more powers generally to the officials in the regions and at points of service.
The departments have been asked to develop a plan to eliminate layers of management and reduce managerial staff by 10 percent. These plans will be implemented starting on September 1, 1991, and the personnel will be reduced over the next two years.

The government will improve the matching of payments it makes with any money it is owed. Revenue Canada, Taxation, will improve the collection of debts owed to governments through its matching and post-assessing activities. These programs are designed to ensure taxpayer equity and the integrity of the tax system. This will be done through the verification of income reported by taxpayers, the examination of claims for deductions and exemptions.
Since 1984, the government has been intensifying its efforts in the area of user fees. Revenues from external user fees now exceed $3 billion, which is more than double the 1984-85 levels. The government is continuing to look for new areas where the application of user fees is appropriate.
Transport Canada will continue to increase the amount of cost recovered from specific users of its services so that the burden of cost on the general taxpayer for these services will be reduced.
February 28, 1991

The government's privatization program has already moved more than 18 Crown corporations and other corporate holdings to the private sector and other levels of governments.
The government will privatize CN Exploration, an oil and gas company created to exploit CN's mineral rights in Saskatchewan.
Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation, PCIAC, will be wound up. Canadian foreign aid in the energy sector will continue to be delivered through the Canadian International Development Agency. This will rationalize Canada's energy aid and result in administrative savings.
Canadian Oil and Gas Lands Administration is being wound up. Residual functions will be taken up by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the National Energy Board, and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Privatization remains a key priority. Given our experience to date, however, and our desire to streamline government operations further, there is no longer a need for a separate agency dedicated to this function. Accordingly, the Office of Privatization and Regulatory Affairs will be dismantled.
The regulatory review functions of that office will be transferred to the Treasury Board Secretariat. Responsibility for the co-ordination of future privatization activities will be assumed by the Department of Finance.

The government firmly believes that numerous tasks are best and most efficiently carried out by civil servants. However, the government also considers it is important to be able to provide services to Canadians in a variety of ways.
That is why we made sure we could contract out certain functions outside the Public Service when that is in the public interest in terms of costs, efficiency or quality of service. The Canadian people expect nothing less, from a government committed to the sound management of the country.
We have negotiations ongoing with the Public Service unions regarding the development of a new labour adjustment policy which will be eliminating barriers to contracting out.
Routine Proceedings
Should it become obvious that it is impossible to reach an agreement before the existing policy expires on March 31, 1991, the government will introduce in Parliament a bill to confirm its right to contract out, thereby eliminating any existing barrier.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
You agree. I can feel it. But you do not want to say so.
Mr. Speaker, our objective is quite simply to give the government enough leeway so that Canadians may derive maximum benefits from the taxes they pay.
Special operating agencies are a major government initiative designed to improve the delivery of public services. In the past year we set up five organizations, including the passport office and the Canadian government printing services, and the results are quite encouraging. By establishing such organizations we hope to enhance the quality of services and increase the over-all value of taxes paid by Canadians.
In his remarks the Minister of Finance referred to the creation of three new agencies: the bureau of intellectual property, a government agency to monitor racetracks, and the Canadian Grain Commission.
We made that decision to implement private sector management techniques more systematically so we can operate on a commercially-oriented basis for enhanced cost recovery.
I am pleased to announce today that the government will give six additional units serving a wide range of clients the status of agency. Here they are:
Office of General Standards of Canada;
Transport Canada Training Institute;
Canadian Administration of Indian Oil and Gas Lands;
Correctional Services Professional Development Program;
Canadian Heritage Information Network;
Canadian Conservation Institute.
I also asked the Treasury Board Secretariat to co-operate with departments to define, assess and create other agencies over the coming year, particularly the kind of organizations which serve the public directly and whose future outlook is most promising.

Routine Proceedings

There should be no ambiguity about the steps we are taking today: they reflect the government's continued determination to reduce the costs of government programs and administrative overhead; they reflect the need for significant changes in the way in which government operates; and they show our commitment to look for the most efficient means of delivering services to Canadians.
These expenditure reductions and other management initiatives form an essential part of the government's broader national agenda: for economic recovery for the continued reform of government.
Change is seldom easy, and significant change can be painful as well as difficult. But significant change in the way the government does business is no longer an option, it is a necessity.
Federal Public Service employees have worked hard to maintain services to Canadians over the last six years of restraint. I am confident that they are able to respond to these further changes and challenges.
Canadians will welcome changes that reduce the size and cost of government while better equipping it to provide the services that taxpayers are entitled to expect.
But the basic message should be clear: we are serious about restraint and we are serious about reform; we are determined to cut expenditures, and to organize and operate the government in a manner that suits the real needs of Canadians.
Hear, hear.

I wish to begin my very brief remarks by referring to part of the conclusion of the text of the hon. minister in which he said, and I quote:

"Canadians will welcome changes that reduce the size and cost of government while better equipping it to provide the services that taxpayers are entitled to expect".
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether Canadians, after listening to the Budget speech made by the Minister of Finance on Tbesday and today's statements by the President of the Treasury Board, really believe they are now better equipped to pursue this country's economic development.
I think most Canadians will share my concern that in the Budget and the documents tabled with the Estimates, the Government of Canada has demonstrated its approval of the Allaire report. I fail to see why the Tory government does not state its position clearly, as so many others have done. If it wants to see this country dismantled, let it come out and say so.
The Allaire report has been questioned by many people. Not long ago, Canadians drew some assurance from the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada had said once again that he was a great federalist. He was, and we have to take his word for it, during the referendum in Quebec in the early 80s. But now, Mr. Speaker, all of a sudden the Government of Canada decides to introduce a number of tax measures that prove to Canadians that the federal government has no, or very little, reason to exist.
Make no mistake. If the federal government admits it no longer has any reason to exist, reflected not only in what it says but also in the measures in this Budget and the notes on how the Budget will be spent, what does this mean for Canadians who seek leadership and are

asking the government to show that it wants to maintain a form of Confederation that will include Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific to the Arctic?

I and my colleagues, in the weeks and months to come will, like all Canadians, be looking very closely at the estimates and at the budget. Already there has been reaction.
It seems to me that many Canadians will be astounded that the government has chosen the budget documents to do exactly what has been rejected by federalists in the Quebec Liberal Party, such as Mr. Paradis, Mr. Ryan and many business people. The Conservative Government of Canada, at a time when the Spicer commission is looking for reasons to keep Canada together, when we are anticipating the Campeau-Belanger report, is accepting the premise that is clearly stated in the document called the Allaire report, and I quote:
The central government will continue to exercise exclusive authority in the following areas: Defence and territorial security; customs and tariffs, management of the common debt; currency and equalization.
That is all that is left of Canada as far as the federal government is concerned in the vision put forward in the Allaire report. That is nearly identical with the vision, if that is what one can call it, that is being put forward in the budget and in the estimates.
Surely there has to be more the Government of Canada can do in indicating its commitment to the future of this country. This is a total abdication of government. It is an admission that it has become irrelevant. I think the implications go far beyond the budget and all the talk we are hearing about what has been improved as a result of moneys being spent or how much an improvement we are going to see in control of the deficit and the debt as a result of restraint.
Those elements will all, undoubtedly, be debated. However, I would be extremely surprised if Canadians who look into this are not struck by the approach the government is taking, of abdicating its responsibility for national programs. It makes no difference what aspect of it you look at; the government has said there really is no need for a strong, central federal government looking at maintaining some national standards and equality among the peoples of this country from coast to coast.

February 28, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The government recognizes, as we all do, that one war apparently has come to an end. On Tuesday and again today, the government confirms that they are declaring war on the regions of the country. They want the provinces now to go to war because it is the only way they are going to be able to survive as a result of some of the measures in the budget and the estimates. They want public servants to go to war among themselves, to fight among themselves for raises and/or jobs.
Surely Canadians expected a budget and an attitude on the part of this government that would reflect the unease that we have as to whether or not we can maintain this nation.
I suspect that the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board are going to bask in the same kind of comments as the Prime Minister did a couple of weeks ago when he made his return to federalism in speeches in Toronto and Quebec City in terms of the comments of Mr. Parizeau, the leader of the Parti Quebecois in Quebec. Mr. Parizeau thought that the Prime Minister's comments were very apropos and made no bones about stating that. I am sure we are going to hear from Mr. Parizeau and probably people who sit in the Bloc Quebecois who are going to tell us that this government has confirmed what they have been saying, that there is no need for a federal government because it no longer has any commitment to Canada, to the regions of Canada, the poor of Canada, the students of Canada or the elderly of Canada.
My colleagues, in the next few weeks, will not derive any pleasure in pointing out where the national government has abdicated its responsibilities.
We talk about trust. It is a quality that many people discuss and many people seek in others and in their institutions. It is not something that is often found these days, but my colleague from Newfoundland yesterday was quoted widely on his description of the budget.
Much of the jargon around these days is related to what has happened in the Persian Gulf. Certainly, if one were to continue in that vein-plagiarism is not always something that I get involved in-surely the prime example of what happened to this government, its lack of direction and its lack of commitment to the country
could be as what some might describe as the "mother of all commitments".
This is what the Prime Minister had to say a few years ago, in 1983. The Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition of course, said: "I have said and repeated dozens of times as far as the Conservative Party is concerned, medicare is a sacred trust which we will always preserve".
I wonder if anybody in the country can be expected to have any trust in what anybody says, if that kind of a comment is weighed in the light of what has happened in this budget and what we find in the estimates with respect to how Canadians can look forward in the next year to receiving services from their government.
The vicious people in this country might suggest that one of the truisms is being proved by this budget and these estimates. The R.B. Bennett syndrome is certainly back among us. Tory times are tough times. It has often been said and there are a few people around who can remember that as an axiom.
Surely this whole notion of being tough, standing up, talking about deficit and restraint in a very dispassionate way brings back memories to those people who either lived through or who have made themselves familiar with Conservative Party policy in previous hard times.
This is the first time that the Conservative Party has had to deal with tough times in this country since the 1930s. I think the elderly in our country are going to shudder when they see the consistency in the approach that this government is using.
The Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board today indicated that they had very limited choices, very restricted choices. There is no doubt that that is true. I think every Canadian understands that we are faced with extremely difficult choices with respect to the level of debt, the burden that that debt places on us and the resulting deficit.
Even when there are limited choices, the choices we do make should be guided by a vision. I am sorry to say, but I believe that this government has taken on a dark vision of Canada, a negative vision, a divisible vision, one lacking in any optimism. It is nearly a scorched earth policy where I suppose, at 15 per cent or so in the polls,
February 28, 1991

you say it does not matter too much so at least we will play to those few people who still support us across the country, who insist on inflicting hardship on the poor, the under-privileged, on disregarding the realities of regional disparity and so on.
There is very little to be upbeat about today. I want to speak for a moment or two because of the last year's experience that I and many Canadians had with the policies of this government with respect to interest rates, monetary policy, the value of the Canadian dollar and so forth.
The conversion on the road to recession that has been experienced by the Minister of Finance is really something to behold because to suggest that the estimates are going to be able to achieve what the Minister of Finance has suggested and what the President of Treasury Board has suggested is unbelievable, especially when you consider from whence it comes. These are the people who said that high interest rates had to be maintained, that high unemployment levels had to be allowed because that was the way to control inflation, so inflation was at 4 per cent, 5 per cent, 6 per cent, depending on which month you choose in the last year or so.
Now, after the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Chamber of Commerce, the National Council on Business Issues and all of these people begged the government to reduce interest rates and had those pleas ignored and refused, the rates have come down. This is the weird and wonderful world of Wilson. With the interest rates coming down, so is inflation. The projections are that if everything turns out according to the budget and the estimates, inflation is going to be reduced to 3 per cent and then 2 per cent, interest rates are going to drop to 9.5 per cent and 9 per cent. Imagine this conversion that the recession has wrought. For months and years we have had people's pleas for interest rate relief and some adjustment of the artificially high Canadian dollar downward fall on deaf ears. All of a sudden a new combination comes forward with lower interest rates, mind you continuing high unemployment and even higher unemployment, and we are going to wind up with very, very low rates of inflation.
I wonder how the people who are going bankrupt and the nearly 1.5 million people who are unemployed are going to respond to this new theory of economics being put forward by the government, the Minister of Finance and the President of Treasury Board, but most significantly, by the architect of much of this.
Routine Proceedings
When interest rates are high, they are kept up there by the Governor of the Bank of Canada. When they drop, we get the royal 'we' and the Minister of Finance says we have reduced interest rates.
The interesting thing is that yesterday, as far as I know, in an unprecedented press conference, the new Crow doctrine had been put forward and that is that we can achieve lower inflation with low interest rates. It is going to be interesting in committee and so forth to find out how this new alliance was forged between the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada because the formula of high interest rates and high unemployment and a high Canadian dollar led to inflation, as I said, at 4 per cent, 5 per cent, and even as high recently as 6 per cent. Now we are going to go the other way. We are going to have lower interest rates and we are going to have lower inflation.
The confusion that seems to be obvious inasmuch as no one understands what is taking place is not the result of people not being able to deal with facts. It is because we are faced with a government that has no commitment, no plan. It is not what I said or predicted yesterday that matters. It is what I am telling you today. But you have to believe that what I am predicting today will come true six months or a year from now regardless of my past track record.
The reason I spoke of conversions is that not so very long ago, because the Minister of Finance likes to relate back to the early 1980s for very obvious reasons, he, in the early 1980s had a great deal to say as well. For example, he spoke about the funding of the established programs and he said that if they decreased, it would lead to a decline in the quality of post-secondary education and an increase in bitterness and confrontation between the federal government and the provincial governments. We do not need a decline in post-secondary education said the then finance critic. We need an increase in the quality of post-secondary education. That was in November 1981.
Speaking of established programs funding, he said that the cuts could have disastrous effects on universities and on colleges and on the operations of hospitals. Let us not make hospitals, universities, and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us not solve those problems on the backs of the hospitals and universities. This is the present Minister of Finance in the early 1980s.

Routine Proceedings
Well, I think that we can probably put as much faith in what the Minister of Finance had to say on TUesday about what is going to be happening a year from now as people generally should have put in the statements of the Minister of Finance when he was in opposition in the early 1980s.
The last point I want to make with respect to the record of the government is what they have had to say about management because that has been, from the government's point of view, its strong suit.
What is unfortunate is that that self-analysis is not shared by outside observers, even among the best friends of the government. When people look at the budget and look at the estimates, I am sure they will keep in mind with respect to management what the Canadian Manufacturers' Association had to say in December 1990. Restrictive monetary policy, large federal sales tax hikes, among others, have directly raised inflation rates and put the economy into a recession and caused large job losses.
Mike McCracken, president of Informetrica says: "The government chose to put the economy into a major recession". Well, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Chamber of Commerce, the National Council on Business Issues all share the view that the government has mismanaged the affairs of this country. The unfortunate thing is that now the people will have to pay.
Hopefully, over the next few weeks and few months we will be able to demonstrate to Canadians that there are many of us who still believe in this country, who still believe in a strong central government, and that not everybody will buy the approach that this government has taken through the back door of fiscal policy and through budget processes and estimates to demonstrate what it was not able to say up front, that it supports that view of Canada where all the national government does is manage the debt, take care of national defence, and be responsible for currency.
I think the people of Canada ask and demand a great deal more than that. I expect that the Government of Canada will find that pitting provinces against the federal government, pitting public servants one against the other, will not be a very appropriate or acceptable way for it to continue to mismanage the affairs of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity, but I cannot say I am particularly happy with this opportunity, because I do not think there is anything in either this budget or in these estimates to make any Canadian happy. I could stand here, I suppose, and say amen to most of the remarks made by my friend from Acadie-Bathurst, but that would not be in the tradition of the House, so consequently I will add a few points.
First of all, I want to say that the estimates, which were tabled in the House today, were put there for the enlightenment not only of members of Parliament but also for the enlightenment of the people of Canada. They should do that. If you take a look at them, you will find they do a considerable amount of confusing rather than enlightening. For instance, there are several neat rows of figures which add up to a particular amount which are said to be the estimates of the Government of Canada. However, last year's Main Estimates which are listed there do not include any Supplementary Estimates, and consequently are incorrect for a good portion of the departments.
If you wish to compare them to the 1991-92 Main Estimates, these estimates do not include a number of commitments made, restraints in some cases and increases in other cases, in the budget just a few days ago. When you have 1991-92 Main Estimates which are also listed and which are also incorrect, these estimates do as much to confuse as they do to enlighten the people of Canada.
As I said before, we have a document with two neat rows of figures, both incorrect. Surely a government that spends as much money as it does on keeping track of funds could do better than that in providing the kind of document that would make it back to the people and to members of Parliament.
There is in this document another confusing element. That is the fact that there is a very sneaky way of reducing payments in any particular year and reducing the amount of money in a particular year. If you look at these estimates, you will find for instance that a certain amount of money is designated over five years. In the budget the other day this was extended to six years.
February 28, 1991

However, the figures in the estimates are still those of the five-year program and consequently are also incorrect. But enough about the incorrect part of these estimates.
There are a number of things in the estimates which need to be discussed. First, there is a real attempt in here, a real direction as far as the government is concerned, to move away from person years. This has been recognized as a concern in the public accounts committee and other groups in Parliament, both on the government side and on the opposition side, of recognizing some concern with the establishment of person years as a method of controlling expenditure. But what the government is doing here now is not reducing the control of expenditures by moving away from person years. What it is doing is establishing a method of privatization which is in the process, or may in the process eliminate, as it has suggested itself, as many as 6,000 jobs, which was threatened in the budget speech. This move away from person years gives the government an opportunity to move into more contracting out.
In the past, when asked, the government has been unable to justify contracting out as a method of saving money, that in fact many senior civil servants consider it more costly than in-house operations, as well as more inefficient. They say this because when somebody is contracted, you have to teach them what they are supposed to do. After the contract is through, you have to fit what they have done into your program. You as the manager in a particular department have to designate people to do that kind of work. It may take as much time as the contract took to get it back into the situation where it is worth while. In the end, you have paid more money for the operation than you would have if you had had the job done in-house.
The minister said in his speech: "Should a new agreement not be reached by the time the current policy expires March 31, 1991, the Government will introduce legislation confirming the right to contract out. This will eliminate any barriers to contracting out that may now exist".
This really is a new wrinkle in labour relations.

Union busting.
Routine Proceedings

The government is going to pass legislation to make sure that the union cannot take action because there will already be legislation in place giving it the authority to eliminate their jobs. That is another factor of contracting out I think we should look at because we know from experience that contracting out by this government has been another way of patronage to its friends. If you increase the amount of contracting out what you are able to do is pay more of your friends for their support.
There is another concern in this process of legislation and reduction of civil servants. The minister said in the budget speech the day before yesterday that there is going to be a trade-off between wages and job losses. As my colleague from Acadie-Bathurst indicated, this pits one employee against the other. It affects the morale of the departments, the morale of the Public Service considerably and it is a way of inviting labour unrest rather than making for people who will work hard and effectively for the government and for the people of Canada.
It is very interesting also that in the minister's speech he indicates that the government House leader and vice-chairman of the Treasury Board will lead the review of the current spending of grants and contributions. In other words, he will take charge of the review of the grants and contributions. That covers every department of the government. Every department contributes a certain amount to organizations that are involved in their particular area. It covers every department and it is a major factor out there of the outreach of the Canadian government to the people of Canada: heritage grants, grants to exhibitions. This is the main contact between the Government of Canada and the people on the street.
It is given to a minister who is going to review it, and he is going to take into account the government priorities.
He is going to improve targeting, promote self-reliance, and reduce overlap. It sounds very good, but this sounds like a way to punish those who do not agree with government policies. That is what was done the last time there was a reduction in grants and contributions. We remember the impact on newspapers, on communications from native groups. It is a way to punish the people

February 28, 1991
Routine Proceedings
who do not agree with the government. Or, is it a method of providing further patronage to one's friends?
One thing that this government is obviously working toward is that in the third year of the government we need some money to expend. I can remember back in the old Liberal days when the senator from Saskatchewan, Hazen Argue, had a considerable slush fund that he used around Saskatchewan, which did not work out particularly well because they elected no members.
However, the development of a slush fund is also part of this government's approach to these estimates. For instance, there is the slush fund of $3.3 billion, which is designated as such. It is a reserve, with nothing attached to it.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Does it say slush fund in the estimates?

Not quite, but it could be; it might say slush fund if one interprets it right. It is there, but besides that there is a number of areas in which the government has funds available.
In forestry, there was a 7 per cent cut across the board, but several agreements have not been put in place. The government is going to make these agreements and then is going to have to go to this $3.3 billion slush fund to find funds to support that forestry development.
In the budget speech the minister indicated a $1.2 billion amount of money for agriculture. It does not appear in the estimates. GRIP and NISA, which people from the west and from the agricultural community will recognize, are not mentioned in the estimates. In the budget speech, $1.2 billion was set aside for agriculture but was not designated for GRIP and NISA.
Therefore, it is there as a slush fund, to buy votes, if you wish, by this government, or to buy votes for a provincial government, as we have had a certain amount of experience with in the past. In B.C., the forestry funds are leading up to the B.C. election; in Saskatchewan, the funds for agriculture from this government are leading up to an election in Saskatchewan.
Let's take a look at the impact of UI. There was a $3.1 billion saving by pulling out of UI, by Bill C-21. They have taken all this money out of the department, and they have taken it out this way: $20.7 million from labour
development, $100 million out of the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
If one did not know the priorities of this government before now, one should be able to get a bit of an inkling by this. Who are they worried about? To whom is this budget directed? Whom is it supposed to help? Obviously, not the workers.
What the workers are getting is increased premiums. If they lose their jobs, they are going to get less training and generally less concern for job development across the country. When they got out of the UI operation a while ago, the Minister of Finance said that the government would cover the shortages in the UI fund.
What happened? In this budget, in this particular instance, he has increased the premiums to make up for any shortages within the fund.
Again, the workers are not being helped by this budget in any way. The cost of unemployment insurance is up 55 cents per $100 of insurable earnings. If they spend half of it on goods and services, it will be 3.5 per cent. Inflation is still up around 5 per cent. CPP payments are being increased. There is nothing in here that would indicate that we should be happy with this budget.
There is no doubt that the priorities of the government show through every area, even where it has proclaimed increases in expenditure. There has been a deliberate move to downgrade services to people. There is a total abdication of the government role of services to Canadians. The tax on medicare via reduced payments to the provinces, the tax on the unemployed by a reduction of training and services, the tax on the workers by UI premiums, GST, CPP increases, continuing inflation and wage restraints, the tax on small business with the GST and UI, and the withdrawal of training from jobs-all these are reducing the impact of government on assisting and making life more bearable for a large number of Canadians.
As need grows, the commitment of government reigns and goes where it will help the multinational corporations make more.
I hope that the committees are able to deal with these estimates. Some of them have not met for a considerable length of time. This is not a people's budget and it is confirmed by these estimates. We should not have
February 28, 1991

expected anything different, because this is not a people's government.
Hear, hear.

Insofar as Environment Canada is concerned:
No Canadian universities and/or other academic institutions have carried out studies, research, or visits north of the 49th parallel in Quebec since 1977, at Environment Canada's request, for the purpose of storing waste from nuclear fuels.
Insofar as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is concerned:

speechtext: Before I call Orders of the Day, I believe the hon. Speaker will listen to a point of privilege.

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given that I had begun to address the matter earlier today, I will not belabour the items that I raised at that time. I will continue roughly where I left off.
I would point out that following discussions with colleagues opposite I will delete from my remarks a number of factual items that perhaps, while relevant, may be seen by some to be collateral and not directly on a point in making a prima facie case.
I want first to refer the Chair-and I am sure I have no need to do it in detail-to precisely what we mean here when we are talking about privilege. I will make a number of references. I will not read all the materials, but I will cite them.
The first item would be the definition of privilege which has been read in this House many times and cited.
I would just refer to two parts of it: that is that the privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and the last portion which states:
-privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent
an exemption from the ordinary law.
I will refer to that later. That citation is from Beau-chesne's and is also contained in the current document called Privilege in the Modem Context published by the House.
The second item I want to refer to is the particular right as one of the rights and privileges that I address here. That specific right is the right to institute inquiries, call witnesses and demand papers. That is a collective right of Parliament and its committees. That right is listed as one of a number of rights also at page 2 of the document Privilege in the Modem Context.
The particular right breached is the right to obtain information through committee orders. I note a second citation in Erskine May, page 69, twentieth edition, where he states that:
When any of these rights and immunities is disregarded or
attacked, the offence is called a breach of privilege -
I maintain that the failure or inability of the minister, in a manner that I will refer to later, is a disregard of that right.
I would also refer to section 18 of the Constitution Act 1867 which codifies, generally, the rights and privileges of Parliament as we knew them in 1867, Sections 5 and 6 of the Parliament of Canada Act which restates them, and section 108 of the Standing Orders which provides the existing codification of the mandate of the House and its committees. I will not read them into the record.
I would point out that in all of these there are no restrictions on the right of Parliament in committees to obtain information other than the limiting subsection referred to in the Parliament of Canada Act and the
February 28, 1991

Constitution which confines those rights and privileges to those existing in 1867 and it is not to go beyond those.
I had hoped to cite a reference-it will take up too much of the House's time given my earlier discussions- of an unfortunate individual in the British Parliament named Mr. Lee who, in the year-roughly 1704-had failed to comply with an order of a committee and was taken into custody by the Sergeant-at-Arms and brought to the House. I will resist the anecdotal recital of that, as amusing as it might be.
My obligation here is to show you a prima facie case that the right and privilege has been breached. The standard I must achieve is not that of beyond a balance of probability, nor is it beyond a reasonable doubt, it is simply a prima facie case and there may, in fact, be justification, as will be put forward as I hope the procedure will evolve here.
The facts on which the claim is based originated in June of 1987 when an inmate of the Edmonton Institution escaped. Following that, the Commissioner of Corrections commissioned a report pursuant to section 14 of the Penitentiaries Act. In December 1989, the report was tendered to the Corrections Commissioner and the report was made public. However, there were portions of the report deleted. There were deletions of pages and paragraphs and two of the conclusions and recommendations in that report were deleted.
In May 1990, the Standing Committee for Justice and the Solicitor General were reviewing the mandatory supervision provisions of the Parole Act and asked for an unexpurgated copy of that report, which has become known as the Weir report. At the same time, the committee asked for an unexpurgated copy of what has become known as the Legere report, a report which dealt with an escape of an inmate in New Brunswick.
In our request for these documents, the committee was unsuccessful. On December 4, in the face of the refusal or inability of the Solicitor General to provide the requested unexpurgated version, the committee formally ordered that the Solicitor General provide this report. I believe I should read that particular order into the record at this time. It reads:
That pursuant to the Committee's own mandate, the Committee order the production before it of the uncensored version of the reports to Correctional Service Canada by one, Mr. Weir, governing the escape of Daniel Gingras in the province of Alberta and, two, by
Privilege
the Board of Investigations concerning an offender (Allan Lfegfere)
unlawfully at large in the Province of New Brunswick, pursuant to-
And here we have the recital of the statutes I had earlier brought to your attention.
-and that the documents be delivered within seven days of the date of this order.
The Solicitor General was not able to comply.
I have with me, and it may be appropriate to table, the written reply of the Solicitor General to the order of the committee. He states that he has carefully reviewed the motion and the request for copies in each case without deletions. He recites a section of the Privacy Act and states:
With regret, I must conclude that the public interest does not
outweigh the invasion of privacy which would result from a release of
the unedited copies of these reports.
In the case of both reports the conclusions, the reasons, and most of the supporting testimony have already been made public.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I ask the courtesy of the hon. member to let me intervene for a moment on another matter.
I would like to make it very clear that in the mind of the Chair, we are in Government Orders. That will have some consequences, perhaps, at one o'clock and I just want to make that very clear to the House. Would the hon. member please continue.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following that reply of the Solicitor General the committee reported to the House of Commons with the seventh report of the committee.
I wish to match those facts with the law stated earlier. In the face of that clear order of the committee which was properly and effectively delivered to the Solicitor General, and in the face of clearly defined rights and privileges of the House, often referred to as the undoubted rights and privileges, the Solicitor General has declined to comply with that order, contrary to the will and wishes of that committee.
Now the Solicitor General has stated that he is prevented from complying because of provisions of the Privacy Act.
The House has therefore been blocked in the completing and the carrying out of its work. We in the committee, collectively and individually, are being denied the information we need as legislators to do our job.

Privilege
The matter has been discussed with the Privacy Commissioner and I feel that the Privacy Commissioner as he then was, Mr. John Grace, should be noted here because he has commented and on May 24, 1990, a very short quote in a reply to a question from our colleague, Mr. Rideout, Mr. Grace says: "And if a legislator cannot see it, my goodness, who is seeing it?"
That is cited from the minutes of the justice and solicitor general committee on May 24, 1990.
I will not review the provisions of the Privacy Act. I do not believe they are necessary to the making of the case here, but I will refer to one thing and that is this: Although I am of the firm view that the Privacy Act does not derogate from the rights and privileges of Parliament, some may argue that it does. I have heard the argument and I believe, although I will not attempt to characterize what the Solicitor General's view is on this, that he is attempting to confront the issue reasonably. In any event if someone were to suggest that the Privacy Act did, I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Privacy Act does not mention Parliament in any of its rights and privileges, and it does not attempt to bind Parliament in the restrictions that it places as part of the general law of the land.
It does however place restrictions; actually it gives rights to certain groups and institutions as courts and investigators. They are specifically given rights to override the restrictions of the Privacy Act. Parliament is not referred to in the act other than a reference to the right or ability of a member of Parliament to obtain personal information where he or she is acting on behalf of a constituent.
I want to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the element I raised earlier in the definition of privilege and the section which states that privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent an exemption from the ordinary law. I commend to you that concept in viewing the effect of the application of the Privacy Act in this.
This is not a partisan approach to this issue. Although many Canadians see the House of Commons from time to time being very partisan, this is apparently not. The committee was unanimous in its order and there have been a number of discussions between members on this
side and members opposite in connection with this. All parties have participated in good faith in those discussions.
It is my view that this motion I make to you today is an assertion of the rights of everyone who put us here in this Parliament.
There are three other quick points I would like to leave with you because I believe they are relevant and will assist you in reaching your decision.
If the committees, as now structured, do fail in their ability to obtain information in the manner that has transpired here, then the committees will fail in doing their work. If the justice committee fails, then other committees will also similarly come up short.
Second, if this is a contest between the rights and privileges of Parliament and the obligations of members of the government-that would be ministers in this House, or let us simply speak of the executive branch of government-if it is a conflict between the rights and privileges of Parliament and the executive branch of government then you, respectfully, Mr. Speaker, have a duty-and I know you understand this-to uphold the rights, privileges and powers of Parliament in the face of that.
Third, if you do find that there has been a prima facie case made that the collective rights and privileges of members of this House have been breached in this instance on the facts of this case, then I am prepared to move to an appropriate motion. However, I would ask that the Chair allow 24 hours, a day, that would permit me and others, including the chair of the justice committee to consult with the House leaders, the committee chairs, and the Solicitor General in constructing a motion that would serve the needs of Parliament and all of the members of the House.
Mr. Speaker, unless you wish me to, I will not address the conceptual issue of the difference between a procedural motion for concurrence and the privilege claim that I make here today. If you wish me to, I could do it very shortly, and it might assist.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
First of all, I want to say to hon. members, and also to the public, this is one of the finest arguments that has been presented to me in my years as Speaker.

I want to say to all hon. members on both sides of the House that I am very aware that this matter is being brought to me after a great deal of co-operative discussion among many members.
I accept very much the invitation of the hon. member to get into a further stage of the discussion. However, if I am reading correctly the hon. member's remarks, it is not necessary at this time. I would ask the hon. member perhaps to conclude and I will then hear the parliamentary secretary.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would only be necessary for me to address this in the event that you felt there was a conflict between that procedure and the privilege procedure. If I might, for the sake of the 30 seconds it might take, I think I will address that.
There was some thought among members and staff here-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: I cannot help but intervene by saying that if we get to that point, I will certainly give you more than 30 seconds.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Well then, I will pass on that in the hope that if further argument is required, I will have an opportunity to address that.
To conclude very briefly, the order of the justice committee on December 4 was a valid, subsisting, uncomplied with order. The order materialized or crystallized a right of all members of this House: a right to obtain information, a right to require production of papers. The right to require that, to achieve that objective, has been breached by the failure of the Solicitor General of Canada to provide the information that was clearly, specifically outlined in the order.
The failure to do it in the way that was cited earlier in the quotation from Erskine May, and I will just note it very quickly: "That when any of these rights and immunities is disregarded or attacked the offence is called a breach of privilege and it punishable-" et cetera. We are not into punishment here. We want to resolve a conflict.
In my view it is clear that the right is there, the privilege is there. The breach occurred, it is unrectified and that you, Mr. Speaker, must find that there has been a breach of privilege, and if I may use the term, collective privilege because it is not my privilege alone, it is the privilege of every member on that committee. That has
Privilege
been breached and the House must deal with that breach.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to add to your compliments to the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River on a very, very thoughtful and well-done argument.
I have had the privilege over the last 11 years of participating in several points of privilege and order. I have to say that the hon. member has made one of the best and more thoughtful arguments that I have heard in some time. I do want to compliment him on that.
Having just said that, I do also want to say that I do not agree with him. He has made a good case but I do not think, in this particular case, that he does have a point of privilege.
I want to come back to that in a couple of moments. But I want to address what I think is the issue here. We really have two conflicting issues that put the House, the committee and the members of this House and I guess to a certain degree the Chair as a result of this point of privilege, in a difficult spot.
The conflict is this. First of all, we have a committee pursuing a subject in which the committee has a great deal of interest. They have pursued it with diligence. They have done a lot of work on the issue. They have come up with a report, or I will describe it as a report, an order in the end, and that is what this House is then seized with.
None of us in this House argue with that process. In fact, we consider that a fundamental part of our parliamentary procedures and therefore, we want to support that tradition, we want to encourage that tradition. We do not want in any way, if possible, to limit the powers of committees. We see them as absolutely fundamental to our process of government and to democracy, as we see it, in this country. That is the first part of this issue.
The second part of the issue, and the one that causes us the difficulty, is that this particular committee has made a request of a minister for a document. Unfortunately, the minister is faced with a difficulty in complying. I think the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River put the right tone on that when he indicated that it was for the minister a difficulty. It was not as though he

Privilege
was trying to be obstructive or difficult with the committee. In fact, all of the signals I have received is that he would like to comply but he is in a difficult situation.
What is that difficult situation? The difficulty is that he has legal advice-which is an interpretation coming out of the Privacy Act-that in fact if he were to respond to this particular request of the committee, he would be in violation of the law and of the Privacy Act.
Of course, any time there is legal argument, there are always two sides, or we would not have a court case; we would simply throw it out of court and it would be decided there.
But in this case, I think we all agree that we are up against legal advice, which certainly appears to be sound legal advice, legal advice which may be debatable but nevertheless is advice that I think all of us would argue has the right to at least have a hearing. It is sufficiently strong advice that it cannot be ignored.
That is the conflict we are faced with. We are faced with a situation where all of us want to see the committee succeed in its work, and support the concepts of committees having the right to information, the right to pursue a subject unfettered. At the same time we then have another principle which we support, that being that we, as parliamentarians, whether we are backbenchers or ministers of the Crown, are not above the law. We have to comply with the law.
I do not agree that the member has a point of privilege. I do not think I have to go into a lot of argument about that, because most of us would agree that in fact he does not have a point of privilege. He certainly has a point of order, and he has a point of grievance or concern, which I think he has demonstrated and argued veiy well in the House. But he does not have a point of privilege.
As you know, when there is a concern arising out of a committee, there is a fixed process according to our Standing Orders-Standing Order 117 being the one that I think is operative-that prescribes for the committee a particular process by which this House is seized with the issue.
So, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe he has a prima facie case of privilege. As I said, he makes a very valid argument, one that I think is fundamental to those of us as members specifically, to those of us as members generally, and certainly to the House and its traditions.
I would therefore put before you what I think would be a reasonable suggestion, one that I hope the hon. member will accept and I think other members of the House will accept; that is, that we refer the issue of the committee's right to pursue information-and the concern that the minister has, were he to comply with the request of the committee-to our Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and Procedures, and that that committee have an opportunity to examine the issue, to report back to this House, and to then not only pursue an issue that is of great philosophical importance to us but also of practical purpose in this particular circumstance.
Therefore, I think that would provide for the House a resolution to a difficult conflict. That having failed, we have no choice. What do we as a House have left to us? We are then faced with a concurrence motion. Of course that puts all members of this House in a very difficult position of how one would vote on a concurrence motion, because we are up against two concepts, two principles, two fundamental values that we see as being important. I think it puts the members and the House in a very uncomfortable and awkward position.
I think the best way to handle it, therefore, would be to refer the issue that my friend from Scarborough-Rouge River raised-and as I said earlier, raised very well-to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. That would give us an opportunity to pursue it, to have a look at it, and to give some advice to this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
We are witnessing today some extraordinarily thoughtful and good arguments. I thank the hon. parliamentary secretary.
I notice that there are others who wish to rise. I will recognize now the hon. member for Edmonton East.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise briefly to bring to the Speaker's attention a couple of matters of which he may not be aware.
I was not able to hear the argument of the hon. member who raised the point in its entirety but rather
February 28, 1991

only the end of it. That reference was made to Beau-chesne's citation No. 625 on page 198 of the fifth edition where it is noted:
(1) Committees may send for any papers that are relevant to their Orders of Reference.
Further, I assume, reference was made to citation No. 626(1) on page 199, where the only stated condition on that is noted and it would seem, in my submission at least, not to be pertinent here.
I was a bit surprised to hear the hon. member opposite who just spoke refer to Standing Order 117, which is a Standing Order governing the maintenance of decorum in committees. I do not know that that is directly pertinent in this instance.
However, the other matter that I would wish to bring to the Speaker's attention is that the document over which this is all being carried on has in some senses already been made public. That was done in the edition of the Edmonton Journal of Saturday, January 6, 1990, in which excerpts from the so-called Weir report were published including sections of that report which were expurgated in the copies of the report forwarded by the minister to the standing committee. I do not know that that will bear directly on the Speaker's decision in this regard, but I would note that that being the case, it leaves members in the awkward situation, especially members of the committee-and I would note, Mr. Speaker, that I was present and voting at the committee on the day the unanimous decision to seek the unexpurgated report was made-of having to rely on reports in a newspaper for the full story of what I think by any reasonable person must be seen as the legitimate contention that the committee ought to have available to itself in the normal conduct of its work.
That that continues not to be the case is I would suggest correctly identified by the member who raised the matter as a matter of privilege.
I sympathize with the Solicitor General in his difficulties, at least his apparent difficulties, under the Privacy Act-

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I am going to certainly allow the hon. member for Edmonton East to continue. In the interest of making sure that all hon. members know some of the background of this, it was my understanding, and I stand

to be corrected, if necessary, that whatever appeared in the press was not done so as a consequence of the minister releasing any information. Would the hon. member affirm that, if that is the case, because I think that is very important in this matter.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to the very best of my knowledge that is in fact the case. The reporter who authored the story that included the excerpts from the report never did identify the source through which he received a copy of that report, but I feel safe in assuming it was not the minister, for some fairly obvious reasons.
Mr. Speaker The reason I intervene on that point is that if a minister had revealed information at one point and then took a position later to not give the information to a committee, it might make quite a difference to the position of the Chair in having to rule on the circumstances. I thank the hon. member for clarifying that particular matter.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL

Of course, were that the case, the matter would be much clearer than unfortunately it is.
I would just like to note that I cannot believe that it was the intention of Parliament in establishing the acts and regulations under which the Privacy Commissioner pursues his or her duties thereby to constrict in any way the privileges enjoyed by this Parliament. Therefore, in this instance, even if it is established that there is a conflict, I would suggest that as the servant of this House, Mr. Speaker, you must in defending the rights and privileges of this House rule that privilege holds sway in this instance.
Mr. Speaker The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, perhaps the hon. member could help the Chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to make a very brief intervention which is really consequent on the excellent one by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River in presenting his case. I wanted to comment on the parliamentary secretary for his very thoughtful remarks, but I had a couple of comments on them and there are two aspects that surprised me and I thought in dealing with your Honour's decision on this matter you might want to consider this point.

February 28, 1991
Privilege
It surprised me that the hon. parliamentary secretary argued that the question of the propriety of the minister delivering the report was an issue. It seems to me that the committees of this House and the House itself have certain powers of a court and courts clearly have jurisdiction in respect to the Privacy Act to receive documents that may be otherwise protected under that act and determine whether the documents in fact should be made public.
It seems to me that a committee of this House must have similar powers. It was, after all, a statute passed by this House that created this act. Parliament has the residual powers of a court for certain purposes. It has power to examine witnesses and call for production of papers and those powers have been an inherent jurisdiction of this House and of its committees from time immemorial. It is one of the privileges of the House to be able to exercise that jurisdiction, in effect the jurisdiction of a court.
The committees of the House are creatures of the House and have similar powers, and I am surprised to hear the parliamentary secretary arguing otherwise. I leave it at that.
The second aspect of his remarks which I think deserves comment was his suggestion that the issue of the propriety of the minister complying with the committee's request be referred to another committee.
Certainly as a member of the privileges and elections committee I would be more than happy to embark on such a study because it seems to me that it is an interesting point if, in fact, he is right on his first one, that somehow the committee lacks jurisdiction to make the determination that a court could make.
If he would like the issue studied, it could be studied there or by the committee that has already done so much work on this issue in dealing with this matter, and I am happy to support that part of the suggestion if your Honour feels it is necessary. But my argument is that I do not believe it is necessary for the minister to be concerned about the propriety of him making the release to a parliamentary committee.
Similarly, he should not be concerned and I am sure he would not be if he were releasing this document to a court of law at the order of the court. I do not know why
the request of a parliamentary committee should be treated any differently than the order of a court, and I am surprised to hear the parliamentary secretary suggest otherwise.
I invite your Honour to look at the origins of parliamentary privilege, to look at the juridical basis for them and the similarity between the privileges of Parliament and the inherent jurisdiction of a Superior Court and determine whether that jurisdiction exists. I think it follows that this document should be produced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I began by complimenting the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River and thanked the parliamentary secretary for his thoughtful contribution. I extend the same compliments to the hon. member for Edmonton East and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.
I think a suggestion has been made which I would like to ask the House if it would be prepared to concur in, a suggestion made by the parliamentary secretary that the matter be referred to the committee of privileges and elections.
It would seem that this might be an appropriate way to resolve this without putting the Speaker in a position where I have to rule on what is clearly a very difficult case. If I were to decide that there were a prima facie case on the basis of the eloquent arguments of the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River, that is if the House supported my notion that there was a prima facie case, it would go to that committee.
We have a suggestion in front of us, and it seems to me very sensible, from the hon. parliamentary secretary from the government side that if there were a disposition of the House to put it in front of that committee that we allow it to go there. In a moment I am going to ask the House if the House will agree to that.
I want to make it very clear that this is a very difficult issue indeed. The subject matter is the release of a person in custody who, during that time of release, overpowered a guard and committed another crime; a matter that strikes right to the fundamentals of our system of justice.
This is a matter of very intense importance. On the other hand, as the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, the Solicitor General is in a dilemma because of an act of this House.

As Speaker, I am not in a position to rule on the interpretation of an act of this House. I am confined to the question of privilege.
The hon. member for Shefford has just joined us, and I hope that he has been able to have been following this difficult, but I think intensely important, matter. He is a member of the House with many years standing, and he might very well want to discuss with his colleagues the general suggestion made by the parliamentary secretary.
If the hon. member for Shefford would like any more time, I would of course extend that to him. He indicates to me that that is not necessary.
I think the appropriate thing to do at the moment is to put to the House the suggestion of the parliamentary secretary which seems to the Chair to be a very sensible one and that this matter be moved by unanimous consent to the appropriate committee.
Is that agreed?

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Is there any discussion on the proposed motion?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
