It is not a motion. I am asking for consent to proceed to put this matter to the committee. It was suggested by the parliamentary secretary. I happen to know there have been discussions that preceded this in the best tradition of this place.
It is not a question of debate. I have to put the recommendation to the House. If there is a question of clarification, then I would, of course, want to hear it.

subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
On that point of clarification, Mr. Speaker, I do not see the difference between whether it goes to the member's committee or the existing committee because I think you are taking away powers of the committee.
The reason I say that is that it could go in camera and discuss any document with the idea that it would not go outside of that. I have seen it done when there were international negotiations and when there are other things. It goes into in camera without press, without anything, just for the information of the members of the committee.
As you take away more and more powers of a member of Parliament-I say this in all honesty because for the first time in my life, I had to send five dollars to get access to information because I wanted it within a month and not within a year from the date of the letter.
Privilege
As our rights here become more and more infringed upon by some ministers who will not answer letters for a year or six months, I feel that Canadians have a right, through their elected representatives, to have access, at least in committee if the committees are meeting, to the business before that committee.
Second, it was in the press, so outside people had access to it that members of Parliament do not have. I just think that if the committee itself is not going to be able to deal with this in camera then I am sure that we can debate it forever before another committee or with a time limit.
It will just cut back on some of our rights as members of Parliament because majorities are in these committees. You, Mr. Speaker, have a right to guard all members of Parliament's access.
I think that whatever happens out of this, we will be watching to see how much the rights of members of Parliament will be infringed upon in access to information.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for South West Nova for her intervention. She is a member who has been here for many years, and I cannot quarrel with much of her thesis.
What we are dealing with here is a very difficult situation. The minister has received advice as a consequence of an act of this House. If that advice is correct, he is put in the position where he says, by law, he cannot give this information. This is the kind of dilemma that ought to be deliberated upon by a committee of this House, because out of that deliberation may come a solution to the problem.
But clearly there is a dilemma. There is no difference of opinion in the Chamber as to the necessity to resolve this dilemma, and there has been the clearest understanding on both sides of just what it is we are facing.
The suggestion has been made, and I sense agreement in the House. Having taken into account the remarks which the member for South West Nova has made, with which I cannot quarrel, what we now have is an opportunity, by consent, to put this matter in the committee that it would go to if it were debated and voted upon in the House, in any event.

Privilege
It seems to me a very sensible way to try to deal with what is a very difficult problem and a matter, by the way, which the public is very much aware of.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL

I was going to answer immediately, but I thought that under the circumstances it would be best if I asked for some counsel on this.

Mr. Speaker, I want to clarify very quickly a point that was made earlier.
Citation 625 of Beauchesne's fifth edition refers to the whole question of the power of committees to summon witnesses, papers, and so on. Citation 625(2) states:
(2) The procedure for obtaining papers is for the committee to adopt a motion ordering the required person or organization to produce them.
That has been done. There is no dispute over that. It continues:
If this Order is not complied with, the committee may report the
matter to the House, stating their difficulties in obtaining the
requested documents. It is then for the House to decide what action is
to be taken.
That to me is the nub of this whole argument. That is why I feel is so essential that we come to an understanding, because if we do not come to an understanding we are faced with a very difficult dilemma.
What do we do? Do we vote to ask a member of this House, a member of the cabinet, to comply with the committee request which advice says he may be breaking the law to do so? That is the nub of the question. That is why it is so difficult for members of this House to make a decision on that.
I do not think it is wise for this House to divide on that particular issue, because I think if it divides we lose both ways. If we make the reference to the committee, then I think we have an opportunity to explore this very difficult problem to make some recommendations as to how we handle those situations should they arise again and I think we then resolve the problem. But if we do not do that, we then are faced with a very serious conflict of ideas, of law and of interpretation of law. That is why I put forward the suggestion that I did, because it is only the House that can decide this issue.
If we do what I have recommended it takes the House out of a very difficult dilemma, and by that I mean members of the House.

In that spirit and picking up a cue again from the parliamentary secretary, I think the hon. member who has raised this matter, after consultation with his colleagues, would perhaps like a moment or two to wrap up, and then I am going to put the question to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am of the view-and I am sure all members are of the view-that what we are dealing with here to some extent may break some new ground. I realize and have some sympathy for the position of the Speaker in single-handedly having to take on this issue framed in privilege. I would like nothing better than to offer, along with colleagues in the House, a mechanism that would lift some of the burdens we have here in dealing with this issue.
I fear being toyed with by procedure; not by people, but the procedures that I have experienced over my last couple of years here I find to be a little unwieldy from time to time. If we were not to deal with the issue of whether or not this is technically a breach of privilege, if we were to accept that there is a problem and to put it to a committee, I am of the view that we should do that only on terms which would make it veiy clear to whichever committee dealt with it that the issue had to be resolved on certain terms. To send it to a committee without terms might, given the way things often evolve here,
Privilege
simply consign the issue to a committee report and the House may never have a chance to deal with it until another issue of a similar type arises.
I would like to suggest to the Speaker that from my point of view as a member who has raised an issue, I would find it acceptable. I would take no umbrage if the Speaker deferred going through the process of making a decision for another day and permitted members on all sides of the House to confer on the framing of an order that would accomplish the goals of the justice committee and hopefully the needs of all members of the House and in the end possibly obviate the need to deal with the technical issue of whether or not this is a breach of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND THE SOLICITOR GENERAL

It is not often that the House gets so close to making up its mind about something and then lets it slip away. I do not know whether to call on the hon. parliamentary secretary, but I am in a position where I know very extensive discussions have taken place.
I am in the hands of the House, and yet it seems to me that the attempt here has been to put this in a committee of this place, which is exactly where it would go if I were to rule that there was a prima facie case of privilege. The committee, of course, could decide whether it is privilege. The committee could decide how ministers are to deal with things which are apparently contradictory between a law that has been passed by this House and the ancient laws and traditions of this place. Sooner or later somebody is going to have to look at this. We have right at our fingertips the opportunity to do so at this point.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague for an excellent speech. It was very good. It is clear from his speech that this budget is long on optimistic forecast but very short on policies that would produce these desired results.
What did this government fail to accomplish over the last six and a half years in the face of what is happening now with this recession and these economic difficulties? What alternatives could it follow in order to help our economy rebound?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her excellent question.
The real point about the budget is not what the government has done; indeed, the budget itself relies almost entirely on statistical smoke and mirrors. What the government has failed to do over the past seven years, as the member has noted, instead of undertaking the kind of economic restructuring so frequently promised, the government has relied on ad hoc cuts which have only served to whittle away the existing apparatus.
February 28, 1991

Instead of addressing the root causes of inflation in the economy, that is to say the structural barriers in the marketplace and in the under-employment of Canadians and of Canadian resources, it has relied on the blunt and inequitable tool of high interest rates.
This is what comes from an economic philosophy which holds that the government has no role in the economy and a political agenda that only serves to aggravate regional, social and economic differences.
In essence, this budget is the logical outcome of this government's refusal to address the fundamental problems in the economy. It is a hamstrung budget, one which demonstrates the extent to which this government, through its own policies, has backed itself into a comer from which it appears unable to extricate itself.
In 1981 the Liberal government of the day employed a counter-cyclical fiscal policy to bring Canada out of recession. By contrast, this government's failure to reduce its deficits over the following seven affluent years, resulting in a $400 billion international debt, means that it is now in no position to undertake such steps. The government projects record growth and productivity based on lower interest rates which, in turn, relies on historical low inflation rates, but it offers no policies which could produce the desired results.
The member has asked what alternative policies might the government have followed. I am certainly not one to argue that the solution to Canada's economic malaise lies in turning back the clock in attempting to re-employ the old tools of state intervention.
Nor would I for a moment argue that the government should attempt to rebuild Canada's trade fortress walls in attempt in some way to isolate itself from the global economy which has emerged in recent decades.
I would, however, suggest that there are ways in which public involvement in the private sector can bring benefit to all Canadians, one where government focuses less on creating economic activity than on creating the circumstances within which economic activity will naturally flourish. That is to say, one which takes as its priority supply-side, as distinct from demand-side, intervention.
The Budget
Under the present government, the foundations that must underpin productivity have been eroded, both through neglect and through growing national divisions. The new rule for the state should be to rebuild these foundations from the bottom up.
Such a strategy, for example, could include working with the provinces to improve educational standards, enhancing our communications and transport infrastructure, removing interprovincial barriers to the movement of goods, services, capital and people and working towards sustainable development by building environmental costs into the costs of production, distribution and consumption.
Industry will need access to long-term, competitively priced capital in Canada if it is to invest in the high value-added sectors of the future. This government should have done more to foster the formation of indigenous capital. Instead, we have seen the government engaging in siphoning off domestic capital and generally weakening the economy. A policy of deficit spending has burdened Canadian industry with the most costly capital in the industrialized world.
This, in turn, has forced industry to turn increasingly to offshore investors, reducing domestic control of the economy and leading to the current balance-of-pay-ments deficit.
Government must also re-examine, in answer to the hon. member's question, the ways in which our financial institutions are structured by looking again at how Canadians channel investment into Canadian industry. We should enable Canadian industry to have access, not only to long-term capital, but to capital that is domestically owned and controlled.
Finally, there is a need to develop mechanisms in our country for enhancing co-operation among business, labour and government and, indeed, among the various sectors of the economy. Unless a broad census can be achieved about the direction the economy should take and the way economic restructuring should occur, there is little hope that Canada's technological, industrial and natural resources can be channelled efficiently and painlessly into what Canada does best.

The Budget

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to rise today to participate in the debate on the budget which was brought down on Tuesday. But before I begin my discussion of that, and I realize I will not have an opportunity to finish before we adjourn, I do want to make a few comments about the events which occurred overnight in the Persian Gulf.
I think we all rejoice to know that hostilities have been suspended. We are waiting anxiously for results from the UN Security Council meetings. They met this morning and will be going into formal meetings this afternoon, with the hope that Iraq will have acceded to the conditions and will ensure that prisoners of war are exchanged, that reparations can be paid and all the elements of the cease-fire are met so that, indeed, it can be a permanent cease-fire and we can get on very challenging task of rebuilding and restoring peace and order in this difficult part of the world.
I think it is perhaps also appropriate this morning to mention that our thoughts are with the people of Kuwait. They have suffered such atrocities and such devastation of their country; we have seen some of that on television over the past few hours. It will take time to not only rebuild the physical infrastructure of their country but also to, I think, rebuild the people so they can once again live without fear or terror which they have been subjected to over these past months. Of course our thoughts are also with the families of those who have been killed or injured during these hostilities.
It is also a time to give thanks. I want to take the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to express my thanks to so many who have worked so hard over these past seven months, and no more so than the 2,500 Canadian men and women who are serving in the Persian Gulf and those who have served during the earlier rotations. They have done an outstanding job and I think we can be very proud of the contribution that Canada has made and Canadians are playing in this situation.
We have seen that some of the personalities on television, Commodore Summers, Captain Dusty Miller, Colonel Lalonde, Denny Fireball Roberts, and all the others who have been so vigilant: on the navy side with the ships and air component, with the CF-18s and those
working in the hospital. There are 550 Canadians who have worked there as well.
My thanks also go out to our Prime Minister and our Secretary of State for External Affairs. When the story of this situation is written, I hope it will be documented in a way that will truly show the outstanding leadership which the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have played throughout; their efforts of diplomacy, and the continuing strength that they have shown to the United Nations and to our coalition partners.
It has been an extraordinary time which has brought nations from all over the world together and to say that they will not countenance aggression and have put actions behind those words.
We give thanks as well to the United Nations because it is perhaps now a renaissance in the history of the United Nations and we hope from the successful role that they have played in this situation, they will become the beacon of hope and really be able to help establish international peace and order.
I want to give thanks to the families of our service personnel. I have had the opportunity of visiting with many of them over this past month in the many bases across the country and many cities and communities. They have been stalwart and strong in their support. I want to give thanks also to the support we have received from so many communities and so many Canadians. It has been overwhelming but I think it is indicative of the kind of Canadian spirit and fortitude to show their support to our people.
There have been many others back here in Ottawa and across the country, many women who serve in the Armed Forces, were not in the Persian Gulf but enabled our activities to take place and who have worked around the clock for nigh on seven months; I want to pay tribute to them as well. They have really done an outstanding job, both on the military and civilian sides.
Now we wait and we hope and we pray that peace will come and that this will provide the opportunity for the world to reflect anew and through the auspices of the United Nations to ensure that we have mechanisms that can maintain peace, order and stability in this world and that we know where there are words there are also actions.

I think Canada and Canadians can stand tall today to know that they have made their contribution to this most just and important end.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me now turn back to our discussions on the budget. I think it was a very important budget. It was our Minister of Finance's seventh budget. We have seen through these seven years a constancy and a consistency. But this budget perhaps more than any other that I have seen over these years really reflects what is so important for us to be doing in this country. It not only responds to the needs of Canadians in this recession, but most importantly it positions Canada for economic recovery in the months ahead.
This government has had to make difficult choices with respect to the Persian Gulf. We now are making the difficult choices which will ensure that Canadians can enjoy economic prosperity, that our young people can look forward to a Canada that is going to have a sound economy in the future.
In order to maintain the standard of living that we have all come to enjoy and in order to provide the very social services that have made Canada an envied nation around the world, we must be able to compete effectively in the marketplace. We know so much of our economy is based on our ability to trade and to be competitive.
Our social services will not survive if Canada does not prosper in the new globalized economy. Indeed, our gains in employment equity-something which I have a great deal of concern and interest in-would be undermined if we were to lose our market share.
Certainly, Canada's economic prospects will be dim so long as we must continue to spend 36 cents out of every dollar on servicing our debt. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the federal government this year must pay $43 billion in debt charges. In fact, it is the largest single spending item. How much easier it would be to respond to the recession and to our options today if we were not shackled by paying $43 billion for what previous governments had borrowed in the past.
This government has no intention of mortgaging the future of Canadians. Through this budget, the Minister of Finance has outlined our plan for recovery. It will be a recovery that is based on some very fundamental princi-
The Budget
pies which I think every individual understands as we do our own budgeting, as we do work with our own financial affairs.
It is a budget that is based upon lower inflation and lower interest rates so that stable prices by the mid-1990s will mean that families will be able to budget with confidence. They can feel more secure. It will mean that the elderly and the unemployed, the working poor, people on fixed incomes will have less fear of the future because they will know that they will not be hit. One of the worst things that can happen is runaway inflation.
The budget is not content simply to tighten our belts while giving us promises of better times to come. This government will help those who have been hardest hit by the current recession. Restraint is not a burden that will be carried on the backs of those in greatest need.
As you examine the budget, Mr. Speaker, you will see that the additional expenditures include more money for seniors, the unemployed and for farmers, who have been particularly hard hit by falling grain prices.
I would remind the House that the expenditure control plan that was introduced in last year's budget, with certain programs exempted from the restraint. Among those were major transfers to persons. Transfers to persons comprise the largest component of federal program spending. It is about a third.
These transfers include old age security benefits, the guaranteed income supplement, spouse's allowances, family allowances, veterans' payments and unemployment insurance benefits.
In other words, these are government cheques that go to the people who are most in need. Particularly in a time of recession I want to assure this House that these are the expenditures that are not being touched.
We have to recognize that our population is aging, and because seniors' benefits are fully indexed to inflation, benefits to the elderly are one of the fastest growing areas of government spending. In fact, the elderly are the beneficiaries of about half of government's spending on social programs.
From my perspective, I know that as a result of differences in life expectancy, the majority of these seniors are women. In fact, when we examined the portion of our senior population over the age of 85, we found that in 1989 there were more than twice the number of women than as men.

That is why in my portfolio responsibilities as Minister responsible for the Status of Women I am very pleased that this budget calls for an increase of $1.6 billion in the amount spent on the elderly. It also calls for $3 billion to be spent on the unemployed. Unemployment insurance continues to be one of the most important elements of Canada's social safety net. The government will continue to use the unemployment insurance programs to provide for those who have lost their jobs.
Just another example of how our recovery will not be sought at the expense of the disadvantaged, I think then we can turn to the new initiatives to help disabled Canadians. Last November my colleague, the Minister responsible the Status of Disabled Persons introduced a strategy to promote equal opportunities for Canadians with disabilities. This budget implements many of those proposals.
The disability tax credit, something that the disabled community has been asking for, recognizes that Canadians with disabilities face higher costs of living and working. It will be increased from $575 to $700 in 1991. As well, the budget recognizes three new disability related expenses in the medical expense tax credit. This change is expected to benefit $35,000 Canadian households at a cost of $20 million. In the past allowances for the disabled, such as subsidized parking and transportation, have been treated as taxable benefits. This budget drops these requirements.
In order to promote more opportunities for disabled Canadians to go into the workforce, and that after all is one of the objectives, one of the cries of many from the disabled community, the business costs of modifications for the disabled, such as wheelchair ramps, will be totally deductible in the year they are incurred. This measure, I believe is fully consistent with this government's commitment to employment equity, a commitment that has helped create new opportunities for the disabled, as well as native Canadians, visible minorities and women.
Let me turn now to another area of the budget and one in my other portfolio that I have a particular interest in; the impact on defence. As my colleagues know, this past year has presented the Department of National
Defence with some extraordinary challenges. Certainly foremost among those has been the conflict in the gulf. Our government's decision to deploy 2,500 Canadians to the gulf region has imposed significant and unforeseen pressures on our national defence budget.
Our servicemen and women have played a vital role in the coalition effort. They are serving Canada, they are serving the cause of international peace and security with great skill and dedication, which I mentioned before. I know the vast majority of Canadians have supported these efforts. They have supported our forces serving in the gulf because the cause that they have served is just. Like previous generations of Canadians in wartime, we must be prepared to pay the costs. Where necessary, these are costs to help ensure the kind of world that we want for our children and for ourselves.
It goes without saying that the Government of Canada, through the Department of National Defence, has a responsibility to support those who have served in the gulf, to ensure that they have the equipment, the training and the support that they need to fulfil their mission. The government has been fully committed to this end. In the Department of National Defence, supporting our force's operation in the gulf is currently our highest priority.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers on Southern Africa met in special session on February 16 in London to discuss Commonwealth policy in light of recent developments in South Africa, including the statement made by President de Klerk on February 1, 1991 which committed the South African government to repeal the remaining legislative pillars of apartheid.
Members will recall that both the Prime Minister and I welcomed the courage and the leadership shown by President de Klerk in making these announcements as we have welcomed the determination of black leaders to work more closely together.
I want to report briefly today to Parliament on the work of that committee which Canada chairs and to seek permission at a later point in the proceedings to lay upon the table a copy in both official languages of the communique.
February 28, 1991

Participating in the committee were Commonwealth foreign ministers from Australia, India, Malaysia, Nigeria, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, the Secretaiy General of the Commonwealth and the former foreign minister of Guyana.
We benefited from the participation of Mr. Thabo Mbeki, Director of the International Department of the African National Congress and Ron MacLean, Canada's Ambassador to South Africa.
The situation in South Africa is changing quickly and profoundly. Many white South Africans, personified by President de Klerk, have re-examined their consciences and undertaken to change not only public policy, but also personal practices and beliefs.
Many black South Africans, particularly Nelson Mandela, demonstrate a generosity and vision that are extraordinary in people so long oppressed. Others, including leaders of Inkatha and the Pan African Congress, are beginning to show flexibility, a willingness to experiment, to compromise. And still other South Africans, black and white, are victims of anger, ignorance, fear.
The world is involved in South Africa precisely because the system of apartheid is so powerful and so deliberate a denial of basic human equality, so singular an instrument of racial prejudice. Just as many South Africans show remarkable responsibility in facing their new challenges, so must the world community weigh and apply our influence with great care. The moral imperative remains: to end apartheid. Now, with change in the air, the question of how we contribute to that goal becomes more complex.
Commonwealth foreign ministers, after extensive debate, reflecting the representative nature of that group, agreed unanimously on a position that recognizes a commitment to real reform, but will only reward actual changes which dismantle the system of apartheid. We believe our strongest sanctions should remain until the system is, effectively, abolished; but that lesser sanctions should be lifted in response to tangible proof of a determination to end apartheid irreversibly.
The committee, therefore, decided to adopt a "programmed management approach" that would reward concrete action in South Africa. The first stage in the program would be reached when the remaining political prisoners are released, when the way is cleared for exiles
Routine Proceedings
to return home, when repressive provisions of security legislation are repealed and when the group areas act, the Population Registration and Land Act are repealed.

These changes may all be implemented by the next meeting of Commonwealth ministers, to be held in late spring or early summer. At this meeting, ministers will look at the kind of progress that has been made and decide whether there are grounds for lifting certain sanctions such as visa restrictions, the embargo on tourism and air traffic and restrictions on official contacts.
My colleagues and I were afraid that the present security legislation would be a major obstacle to political freedom. We appealed to the South African government to stop detention without trial, to lift restrictions on public meetings and to grant South Africans the universal right to freedom of assembly, freedom of expression and due process of law. The record must show substantial progress on the return of exiles and release of political prisoners by April 30 this year, as agreed in the announcement from Pretoria last August.
The committee also addressed the question of sporting contacts. In future, the embargo on sporting contacts will be treated independently from other sanctions. The committee agreed to be guided by representative sports bodies at South African, African and, in the fullness of time, international Olympic levels. These organizations will provide the signal for the re-admission of South African sports to international competition. Indications are that this will probably take place on a sport-by-sport basis.
The committee agreed that Commonwealth support and encouragement for the unity talks in South African sports organizations are a high priority.
In order to support the process of negotiated change, the committee further agreed to provide constitutional expertise and funding for research and conferences which will contribute to the birth of a new, non-racial and democratic South Africa. For its part, Canada is providing $1.8 million in 1990-91 and has earmarked $2.3 million for this purpose next year. Canada has also committed $5.8 million to assist with the return of exiles and released political prisoners.

February 28, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The committee also welcomed the interim report of the Expert Group on Human Resource Development for a Post-apartheid South Africa, which the Conference of Foreign Ministers established at our Abuja meeting. That committee is chaired by a Canadian, Mr. John Harker. We endorsed the expert group's call for an enhanced Commonwealth program of training and work placement to prepare black South Africans to take senior jobs in a post-apartheid government.
The meeting demonstrated the continuing unity of purpose of the Commonwealth. The concept of the "program management approach" marks an important policy development for the Commonwealth and for the international community. Sanctions have been crucial in bringing about the changes that have occurred to date, and will go on being crucial if the destruction of apartheid is to be ultimately assured.
South Africa is starkly different from what it was. There is a long way to go. Canada has played a steady, constructive role in moving that change forward, and we intend to continue on that course.
With the permission of the House, I would like to lay upon the table a copy, in both official languages, of the concluding statement of the committee which met in London on February 16.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for presenting this statement to the House. It comes at an important time. It is worth observing that, for the past several months, we have all been quite obsessed and preoccupied with the events in the gulf and perhaps have not given the importance to other international events that have been taking place.
It is important that this House, which over the years has expressed a strong interest in the issues of South Africa, in general part, has provided consensus on the approach to be taken. I think virtually all Canadians have had general support for the thrust and direction that
have been taken by successive governments toward the actions of South Africa. It gives us an opportunity to make a brief re-examination of the circumstances that now ensue as a result of the quite important statement that President de Klerk offered on February 1.
In this, I would like to join the Secretary of State in also congratulating the de Klerk government for the initiatives that they are taking. In some ways, they are courageous.
We know that there are very strong political forces in that country that are railed against the present government and are trying to impede that progress.
Equally, I think we must congratulate the efforts being taken by Nelson Mandela and the African National Congress and the way they are changing their own policies. I think we are all encouraged by the recent meeting between Nelson Mandela and Buthelezi in terms of coming together to provide a more common front in South Africa to allow some kind of progress toward reform in which the black majority of South Africa can work in a more directed way.
Also, I think it is important to pay some tribute to the many Canadians, particularly those in the churches and non-governmental organizations who over the past several years have maintained this as an issue of priority and have provided, as we all know, a continuing sense of encouragement and support for the actions in Parliament.
I think they can begin to now see some fruits of those long years of struggle when it looked like no progress was being made. In fact, I think we can say that two or three years ago, anybody in this House who would have predicted a South African government making the announcements about the changes in the apartheid laws that were made on February 1 would have considered it to be impossible.
The predictions at that time were that we would be facing a horrible feeling of violence and racial conflict. It looks now that there is a good chance for a peaceful transition, not an easy one-it will not be easy-but at least a peaceful one.
February 28, 1991

Again, we want to offer our continuing support as the Official Opposition to any efforts that can be made both to the Commonwealth Foreign Ministers and the very important work that they are doing.
It is my own belief that the Commonwealth Foreign Ministers group is perhaps the most important group dealing with the issue of apartheid at the international level.
I would hope that the Secretary of State, because he is chairperson of that group, might use that position to also make the views known directly to the European common market ministers, who were meeting at about the same time, about the need to follow what they called their "plant management approach". I think it is very important that this area work in concert.
If I might be allowed just to still raise some words of caution. Time is running out. We know that there must be a constitutional meeting by 1991 and I believe the mandate of the de Klerk government begins to run out by 1994.
If significant changes are not taken and we do not encourage those changes then we might find ourselves in a position where all the progress that has been made up to now will be lost. It is very important that we consider the kind of dilemma that the Secretary of State has offered.
How do we, in fact, maintain the constant pressure of having applied sanctions over the years and at the same time provide encouragement? It is an extraordinary act of international skill and diplomacy that we maintain this balance.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, if you will give me a small moment's indulgence to comment on sanctions themselves-it is a topic much discussed in this House for the past several months-I think the Secretary of State himself has recognized sanctions can work and can be effective. They have worked in the case of South Africa, not with the speed of military action but certainly without the kind of side effects that we have seen so dramatically displayed.
It is important to recognize that because sanctions must not be discarded. They are an important tool in the arsenal of the international community coming to deal with things of the serious nature of both apartheid and of aggression. I would hope that we would sit back and reflect more carefully about how useful and effective sanctions are.
Routine Proceedings
In that case, we agree with the approach being taken, that the existing economic sanctions must be maintained until we see action taken to underline the words. We support that and will continue to give the government support in that area.
I would like to make, if I might, a major recommendation to the Secretary of State that he could communicate to his colleagues. We think it is also important at this time that a serious review be done in Canada about what has taken place in South Africa, and in particular, what kind of criteria or steps would be taken to further induce, encourage or support the reforms that are under way.
I think the Standing Committee on External Affairs might be the proper body, so it would not be just an inside decision of the minister and his advisers but would give Canadians an opportunity to come and be heard and to make their cases in terms of the direction they would like to see the future Canadian government policy take, as this is a crucial area.
I would strongly urge the minister to communicate with the standing committee chairman, as we will, that this kind of review be undertaken as one of the priorities so that when he goes to the meetings on April 30, and perhaps to the First Ministers' meeting in Harare, he can carry with him and the Prime Minister the full weight of a general basis of Canadian opinion and they can express it at that point in time.
I have one other point to make, if I might, Mr. Speaker, before I leave. I would like to offer an observation. One of the unique and important contributions that Canada has made in the whole debate over South Africa has been the support for the front-line states. I think we, among many other countries, have given special attention to their needs. What we must do now is realize that their needs are even greater.
In talking just recently to one of the ambassadors of the front-line states, he told me that his own country since the inception of the gulf war has suffered a net income loss of $800 million and that that kind of experience is repeated in the other front-line states, in fact in virtually all the African states.
It is very important, therefore, that when we come to the question of how we deal with the economic consequences of the gulf war we recognize that there is a host of nations-front-line states of Africa among many others-that are suffering deeply and terribly as a consequence of this war. It is going to be a real

February 28, 1991
Routine Proceedings
responsibility and obligation of countries like Canada to come to grips with how do respond.
I say that with great sadness, looking at the budget of Tuesday. It is again a further restraint or restriction on our ODA budget. It does not give us the kind of manoeuvring room or the kind of resources we need. I also look at the kind of negative response that was given by the government to the committee report on Third World debt, wherein the recommendations were virtually all rejected.
It would have been another important way in which we could be moving to provide a more active and positive source of relief for those states. That is even more important now as a result of the war. I do not think the war is the only pretence, because the problem was always there.
I would again urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who in the past has shown particular leadership in dealing with the front-line states, to recognize that they now face even more serious problems than they faced six or seven months ago.
In that case we would say there is a lot of work yet to be done. We in this Parliament can help this government to provide that work both by using the full resources of Parliament to help develop the future policies which the minister can use to advise his Commonwealth colleagues but also to come to grips with the continuing and enfolding tragedy of some of these states, both in those related to South Africa and in the entire African continent, that are facing very troublesome and difficult times.
We appreciate the opportunity to make this statement and to say to the minister that we hope to be able to continue to work with the government not always in concert with his views, but certainly with the general thrust that we must have apartheid come to an end, and the sooner the better.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party to express our strong support for the Commonwealth foreign ministers' decision to maintain sanctions against the South African regime.
I also want to signal the contribution that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made in his role as the chairperson of that very important and crucial body. I also want to associate myself with the remarks of the member for Winnipeg South Centre with respect to the very difficult situation facing the front-line states. My hope is that our government will recognize that and will continue to provide the kind of support they so desperately need, particularly in light of the developments in the gulf.
I was also pleased to hear the remarks of the member for Winnipeg South Centre with respect to the importance of sanctions. Unfortunately it was not until the mid-1980s that the Government of Canada finally took the step of enforcing firm and effective economic sanctions on South Africa. I very much regret that predecessor governments did not take that important step, that they allowed South Africa to continue its system of apartheid without in fact implementing those kind of firm sanctions that should have been implemented long before the mid-1980s.
We in the New Democratic Party share the view of the African National Congress, the Organization of African Unity, the African Commonwealth States, and human rights groups here in Canada and South Africa that while the South African government has made important preliminary steps toward dismantling apartheid, the foundations of this repressive and racist system remain untouched.
I want to join in commending the Canadian NGOs that have been so active in this area, the many individuals who have worked hard through the voluntary fund and elsewhere for these long overdue changes.
As one of those individuals representing a very important organization, Anne Mitchell of the International Defence and Aid Fund for South Africa, recently wrote: "Repression continues. South Africans continue to be detained and imprisoned, harassed, tortured, and even killed because they are known to oppose a system of apartheid".
There were more political trials in 1990 than in 1989 despite the reforms which have taken place. Political prisoners remain in jail. Political exiles remain outside their country. Repressive legislation remains on the statute books.
February 28, 1991

I would note that it is not just a question of legislation, but issues such as housing, education, training, literacy, unemployment and health must all be addressed in South Africa as well. The fact, for example, that the per capita spending on social services in the last year, in 1990, was five times more for whites than it was for blacks in South Africa.
I would hope that in a new South Africa, in a democratic South Africa, there would be a major commitment to attacking the desperate poverty of blacks, the fact that some 70 per cent of blacks live below the poverty line, by addressing the inequitable distribution of both land and wealth in that country.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is well aware also of the serious concerns that have been raised by Amnesty International on the question of the existing security legislation and abuses under that legislation in South Africa. Indeed, at the current meeting of the 47th session of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, at which Canada is very ably represented by Ambassador Reynell Andreychuk, serious abuses of human rights were documented by Amnesty International. I would hope that they would continue to be addressed vigorously by our government.
We believe that the existing sanctions must remain in force until President de Klerk has fulfilled his promise to release the remaining 2,500 to 3,500 political prisoners who are held in South African jails and to allow the some
40,000	political exiles to return home freely.
As well, South Africa's strict security legislation must be revoked, particularly the Internal Security Act which provides for detention without trial and the banning of public gatherings. Most important, existing sanctions must continue until blacks are guaranteed full democratic rights in the South African Constitution; in short, until there has been irreversible change in the evil system of apartheid.
We support the concept of a constituent assembly. I would commend to the South African government, as I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs would, the experience in Namibia which I think is quite relevant in this context. Long before the convening of a constituent assembly in Namibia, all of the political parties in Namibia were able to agree unanimously on constitutional principles and later, even during the heat of their election campaign, they again agreed unanimously on a code of conduct. I would hope that that kind of example is one that would be followed by South Africa.
The Budget
I would hope as well that they would address the homeland system, which is an expression of the system of apartheid and some of the measures that are taken to ensure that all people of South Africa, including those in the so-called TBVC states, participate fully in the future of their country.
While we commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs on his recent important work at the Commonwealth conference, we strongly encourage him not to abandon Canadian sanctions until all of these conditions have been met.
I would suggest in closing that we owe nothing less to the black majority of South Africa, to their courageous leaders such as Nelson Mandela, and to the memory of all of those who have died in the struggle for democracy, for justice and freedom in South Africa, including Steve Beeko imprisoned in 1977, those who died at Sharpeville, those who died at Soweto, and those who continue to die until this evil system has finally been eradicated.

Mr. Speaker, before Question Period, I was just talking about the impact of the budget on the Department of National Defence. I would just like to conclude those remarks by indicating that the costs of our operations in the gulf have been running about $105 million a month. We have absorbed much of that within our regular budget. We did have a supplementary estimate in the fall, about one-third of which was directly related to the operating costs in the gulf.

The Budget
In this budget there is provision for $600 million to look after some of our costs, some of which will be incurred in this fiscal year, but not paid for until the following year. We also anticipate there will be some continuing costs over the period of time.
I have already heard from colleagues on both sides of the House that perhaps that money will not be needed and that they want it for their particular programs. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that DND will be using that money as frugally as possible. Any remaining, however, will be going back to reduce the deficit, not for any individual programs that members might promote. I want again to assure that we do have the funds to look after the men and women, the equipment and the transportation that will be required during this period.
Finally, coming back to the budget, I think all members of this House, no matter which side of the House they are on, would want to congratulate the Minister of Finance. What he has done is walk the very fine line required in this time of recession. We know that times are tough, and we know that many Canadians are suffering in one of the worst economic downturns in years.
But in responding to those troubled economic times, the Minister of Finance has avoided hampering our economic prospects for tomorrow by imposing band-aid solutions. He has responded, first of all, by helping those Canadians who are hardest hit by the recession but, more important, he has positioned us for an economic recovery that will take advantage of low interest rates, low inflation, and new opportunities for Canadians.
Who will benefit as a result of this budget? All Canadians will benefit. As we emerge from the recession with stable prices, with government spending under control, perhaps the greatest beneficiaries will be future Canadians, our children. They will thank us for taking strong measures now to reverse the mistakes of the past and pave the way for tomorrow's opportunities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some questions for the associate minister, which arise from her comments about defence spending and the budget.
I personally was a little confused about comments in the budget that came down yesterday. I went back to the expenditure noted in the 1990 budget to find that last year we had budgeted under defence $11.87 billion and for 1991-1992, this year, we were to have an expenditure of $12.46 billion. In the budget that came down this week, we see the budget for this year instead of $12.46 is $12.7 billion. However, we did have in Supplementary Estimates, a vote which increased the defence budget to cover the costs of the gulf war.
Repeatedly I have asked at the joint meeting of external affairs and national defence, which has been sitting while the House was adjourned, about the cost of the gulf war. I have heard the minister of defence say that all the funds that were voted in the expenditures in December covered all the costs of the war up to and including the end of March 1991. But when those Supplementary Estimates were voted in December, we were not at war at that time. We know that we have had additional costs since then. He assured me that all those additional costs were included in the Supplementary Estimates.
My confusion is: if they estimated that was to cover us up to the end of March and we are presumably today, thanks be to God, seeing the end of that war in the Gulf, I cannot understand the need for $600 million in addition to the regular budgeted additional funding to defence this year. I wonder if the deputy minister could explain that, please, the associate minister.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has the same difficulty many people have. It is the associate minister. The deputy is of course our very fine deputy, Mr. Fowler, who gives us excellent advice on so many issues related to defence.
Just to bring us back to what we are talking about in the defence budget, we have received 5 per cent nominal growth in the defence budget, this year over last year. That is not including the $350 million. That did not become part of our base, Mr. Speaker, so you take our old base and add 5 per cent. There have been some adjustments because we no longer have to pay GST. That

came out of the budget, but we basically have $12.8 billion for the coming year.
The $350 million which was allocated in the Supplementary Estimates was not all for gulf related expenses. There was expenses for Oka in that, $16 million; some for the operations in the gulf; and some for capital. For example, $100 million was for the acquisition of the additional Hercules aircraft, the transport aircraft. Some of the additional $600 and million will also probably go toward that capital will be required, but there will be expenses that will flow into next year. We have incurred expenses that I am sure will not get paid for until the coming 1991-92 fiscal year, and the expenses have been going up.
The deployment of the field hospital was not taken into account in our earlier estimates, so our costs have risen, running now at about $105 million a month. We have been accommodating about $70 million of those in our regular expenditures and about $35 million we are looking to come out of the additional allocations. All the bills are not in; it is hard to say. We do not know what the costs are going to be to bring our people home or how long they are going to be there. The hospital, for example, might stay for a period of time if there is a need for it, if the British or others require it. There may be a need for the ships to remain for a period of time.
Really until we see how things unfold at the UN Security Council, what the future is going to be, it is a little hard for us to predict what those kinds of expenses are going to be. But we will be monitored on the $600 million. We are not allowed to spend it on just ordinary things. They are going to make sure that it is used for its purpose. What we do not spend goes back to reduce the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the associate minister. The first springs from, of course, the effect of the end of the gulf war for which we are all, no matter what our differences on how we arrived there, grateful. All of us have also shared a great admiration for the professionalism and competence of our forces there. We differed on the instructions the government should have given them, but we supported their role in the sanctions and supported them in their professionalism and on the work they have done.
The Budget
There is now the question of what happens next. The Huron is half way there. The Restigouche has orders to sail on March 5, which is coming up very quickly. The people of our area, greater Victoria, are obviously very concerned as to whether the orders will change as a result of the outcome of the war. The government, it seems to me, owes it to the families and to those who are on board those vessels to make an immediate decision as to whether those orders should be changed or whether they should be confirmed.
Let me say that the situation is such that it would seem to me imperative that the government not only review the orders quickly, but in fact make a change in the orders. Our forces would no longer face an enemy that is armed and equipped to attack the naval forces in the gulf.
Sanctions may be continued, presumably for a relatively brief period of time, in order to enforce the remaining UN resolutions, but sanctions will not require a significant military force from countries outside the gulf in order to enforce those sanctions. The naval forces of Bahrain, Qatar and the other countries in that region are entirely capable of enforcing the sanctions in the current situation.
We would call on the government to make an immediate decision, to bring our forces home and to reverse the orders given to the Huron and the Restigouche.
Let me ask one other quick question. Our forces who served there, all of our forces who served there, served in a veiy dangerous situation. Our CF-18 pilots actually were in effect in combat, and our naval forces worked under the threat of Iraqi missiles and planes.
The war veterans legislation provides that veterans of other wars be given pensions under that legislation. It will require an amendment to the legislation to cover the veterans of the gulf war.
I would ask the minister to make a commitment on behalf of the government, that legislation will be introduced to provide that those who served Canada in the gulf be treated as veterans of other operations.
While the minister is on her feet, would she also make a commitment to those who have served in peacekeeping, because they too have served Canada in a dangerous and risky situation?

The Budget

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions there.
First of all, I believe it would be imprudent to make decisions today about the arrangements for our ships until we know the outcome of the Security Council deliberations which are going on as we speak. Until we know for sure that there will be a permanent cessation of hostilities and until there has been some agreement on what the future regime is going to be with respect to sanctions or continuation of any kind of a presence, we want to continue to be ready to deal with the rotation of our ships. The Athabaskan and the Terra Nova have been there. We have committed that we are going to bring them out as quickly as possible.
If for some reason there should still be a need for a Canadian naval presence over the next couple of months, we would want to make sure we had our other ships there so the Athabaskan and the Terra Nova would be relieved and be able to come home, as we have promised them.
At this time, we have, in fact, told the Huron to continue on its voyage. We are, of course, reviewing the situation. Our senior military advisors are in touch with our commanders in the field, with the members of the other coalition forces to assess just what should happen and will make other decisions relating to these matters as quickly as possible.
Until we have all the facts, until we have all the information, I think it would be foolish to make precipitous decisions.
I might say that from my understanding, the sailors ready on the Restigouche probably want to go. Even if they got down to Hawaii and had to come back, I think they would probably prefer that rather than staying in port.

speechtext:
I would be pleased to reply to my hon. friend from British Columbia.
I know that in British Columbia they often enjoy fed-bashing. I am not particularly keen on provincialbashing. But I must say that in this instance, the premier is wrong. This budget is good for British Columbia. After all, British Columbia's economy is based on trade and a viable, vibrant economy and low interest rates, low inflation, which are absolutely critical to the expansion of the economy of British Columbia. Those are the kinds of initiatives we are undertaking.
The initiative in this budget to legislate spending limits is the kind of thing I would expect the province of British Columbia to applaud. It would seem to be consistent with their philosophy. The provisions in this budget to set up a special fund into which the net revenues of the GST will go, guaranteeing that they will go to reduce the deficit, not for other programming expenditures; a fund to which the profits from privatization will go; a fund to which individuals can contribute to help reduce the deficit. These are the kinds of measures that the province of British Columbia should be applauding, because they are the kinds of measures that will ensure that we have economic growth and that we have the entrepreneurship flourishing in British Columbia.
One other thing. Just prior to the budget I had the pleasure of announcing in Vancouver, that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, was approving amendments to the Income Thx Act which would allow for the establishment of international maritime centres. This is something the province of British Columbia has been asking for and something I have had the honour, as the minister responsible for the Asia-Pacific initiative, to work on over the past two years. That initiative by my colleague, by this government, is going to result in a considerable number of jobs, some of which have already been announced this week when the first company announced it is moving its mine and management operations from outside Canada to Canada, to Vancouver, bringing 80 jobs. That is one week. We have lots more to come.
February 28, 1991

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to hear Liberals and Conservatives arguing with each other about who has responsibility for the deficit. It is like two Mafia families arguing with each other about who has been able to commit the most robberies in their respective jurisdictions.
The fact is that the deficit owes its origins to the policies of both of these parties over a great many years.
This is a budget allegedly preoccupied with addressing the problem of the deficit. TTiis is a budget which calls in glowing terms for all Canadians to do their part. But the big corporations that finance the Conservative Party and that financed the promotion of the free trade agreement have emerged unscathed and unchallenged. They apparently are not part of the larger Canadian community that is called upon to face economic reality and pitch in.
Yet everyone else is being called upon to contribute to a debt problem that has its origins, as I said just a few minutes before, in the tax breaks that these same people, these same large corporations, received over the last 15 years, many of which-that is to say these tax breaks- had their origins in the policies of Liberal governments.
This budget eliminates not a single such tax break. So the rich will continue to get richer, the poor will continue to get poorer, and middle-income Canadians will increasingly be taxed until they, too, are poor.
The boys over at the Business Council on National Issues will be breaking out the champagne. Others, and not them, thank God, are called upon to help their country. Oil companies whose profits have risen since the gulf war also get off scot free while working Canadians are asked to pay more taxes to help pay the cost of other working Canadians fighting in the gulf.

The Budget
Average Canadians are to suffer a tax hike through increases in Unemployment Insurance premiums, a measure that will also hurt small businesses.
The unemployed, themselves, see their job creation programs chopped: $100 million from the Canadian Job Strategy.
Those who could benefit from new social housing see that program cut back.
Provinces are hit with the next stage in the step by step withdrawal of federal commitment to cost-shared programs and by the limiting of deductibility of provincial payroll and capital taxes. A revenue neutral measure, so the Minister of Finance says, that could therefore only be vengeful in nature and hardly a contribution to national unity. And all Canadians who use provincially administered services like health care will become the victims of further cutbacks in their respective provinces.
Meanwhile, the rich will continue to be able to afford to send their children to private schools to avoid the effects of cutbacks in education. They will continue to be able to fly to U.S. hospitals to avoid waiting lists for surgery in Canadian hospitals increasingly overcrowded and burdened because of under-funding owed to the fact of federal cutbacks in EPE
And, in between, they will also be able to enjoy the over-all fact that their debt burdened country is still not asking them to contribute in the form of a truly progressive income tax system, in the form of increased capital gains taxes, in the form of wealth taxes, or heaven forbid, not being able to deduct their business lunches.
They may also take comfort in the fact that the dividend tax credit remains and that the corporations that many of them work for or own will continue to receive the subsidy of the 5 per cent federal sales tax credit, the subsidy for business lobbying and other political activities and the subsidy for Canadian multinationals investing overseas.
Nor will they have to fear the dreaded minimum corporate tax. Real estate developers, in particular, can relax and continue to enjoy all the breaks that enabled so many of them to become millionaires at taxpayers expense.
These people, all of them great critics of the welfare state, but not a peep out of them when it is they who have their nose so deep in the public trough.
A budget truly committed to deficit reduction and burden-sharing would have asked the corporate sector in this country to put up or shut up about the deficit. Indeed, there were some indications prior to the budget that the business community was asking for it, that they were asking to be asked to contribute, but they were not.
Instead, we have a budget that by its own words is more committed to "tax competitiveness" than "tax fairness".
Unfortunately, "competitiveness" is the euphemism employed by Conservatives for the growing immorality and unfairness of our tax system, recently capped of course, by the GST.
One can only suppose that the tax system in various military oligarchies, like Guatemala, where income tax itself is seen as radical, is the ideal of tax competitiveness to which good Conservatives aspire. The long-range goal of the hemispheric free trade agreement makes this more than just political rhetoric. Not for the Conservatives, the many European examples where social justice and competitiveness have gone together.
If a budget is more than just a tool for managing the economy, if it is also a statement about the values that inform the organization of that economy, then this budget is a failure on both counts.
I am glad to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the House because he said he did not want to miss the speech and I can understand that because I hope to talk about the whole question of Established Programs Financing and the future of medicare and, perhaps, while he is here I will have the opportunity to engage him in conversation about that.
I think what is happening to Established Programs Financing and to the programs which it it intended to finance, i.e. medicare and post-secondary education, is indeed worthy of all the rhetoric which has been used to describe the government's budget in the last few days.
The problem is that there is no one decision which, in itself, is the end of medicare. It is a bit like the story of the frog which will allow itself to be boiled to death if you simply turn up the heat one degree at a time. There would be no point at which the frog feels the increase in the heat enough to jump out of the boiling water. Yet inevitably at some point, the frog will be done so to speak and dead.

This is the case with those programs in this country which are being, over time, step by step, starved to death by the federal government. This process started not with the Conservatives but with the Liberals in 1982. It was former finance minister Allan MacEachen who was the first finance minister to unilaterally change federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
The last time the federal-provincial governments agreed on this sort of thing was in 1977. I see the hon. member for Mississauga here. He will know what I am talking about. It was in 1982 that the Liberals unilaterally changed and cut back on federal transfer payments to the provinces under the rubric of the established programs financing, a move which at the time was denounced as the most dastardly deed possible by the Conservative opposition.
Yet unfortunately, what the Liberals did at that time set a precedent which has been followed religiously, and not just at the five year intervals of renegotiation, but in almost every budget, of unilateral cutbacks to federal transfer payments to the provinces.
There is no point at which in cutback after cutback after cutback we can say: "This budget kills medicare." What we are able to observe from 1982 onward-and an inescapable fact is that for most of the years since then the Conservatives have been in power-is a trend which if not stopped and reversed will eventually lead to the destruction of medicare as sure as I am standing here.
One cannot expect the health care system to be carried by the provinces, which are being asked to carry a larger and larger share of the burden. The share that the provinces have been asked to carry has grown. They may have benefited in the late 1970s and the early 1980s, but from 1982 on and particularly from about 1984, their share of the burden has been increased and their ability to carry the health care system has been affected.
What will be the results of that? Eventually, people will try to find ways; that is, provincial governments will try to find ways to supplement the reduction in funding and particularly if they are Conservative provincial governments, they will look for various ways of getting private money into the system.
The Budget
That will happily coincide with their ideological views in the first place because many of them have a philosophical objection to medicare. And so we see everything falling into place, not to mention the effect of the free trade agreement in the long term on medicare.
One must do some analysis to see all this, but it is there. That is why I feel no intellectual or political embarrassment whatever in getting up and saying: "This budget is part of the end of medicare." Not tomorrow, not even next year, but it is part of a process that will eventually lead to the end of medicare. I rest my case with respect to that because I have other things I want to say.
I want to go back to the question of tax loopholes.
It seems to me that this is the glaring economic and moral flaw in a budget which calls upon everybody to sacrifice, that not one single sacrifice is asked of the corporate sector in this particular budget. Not only that, there are more benefits to come for the corporate sector. Just the other day, the Minister of Finance released draft legislation with respect to providing a capital gains tax exemption for people who have had their money tied up in trusts over this 21-year period that began in 1972 and which ends in 1993. The government has brought in draft legislation which proposes to extend the 21-year exemption for the taxation of capital gains from trusts until the last beneficiary of the trust dies. Under current rules, the government would have collected billions in revenues from trusts starting in 1993.
The current legislation, implemented in 1972, requires trusts to include in their income capital gains every 21 years. This legislation would allow the trust to extend the 21-year exemption, as I said, until the last beneficiary dies. The billions saved by trusts would be a gift to the top 1 per cent of wealthy Canadians who benefit from these trusts.
This exists at the same time as all these other measures in the budget which scapegoat people who work in the Public Service, the unemployed, and a variety of other people, and make them out to be the cause of the deficit. One of the causes of the deficit-a principal cause of the deficit-is the tax expenditure account that government after government refuses to significantly change.

February 28, 1991
The Budget
I see the member for Mississauga South. He will recall that in 1979 when the Conservatives came to power, they released a thing called "The Thx Expenditure Account", because they had promised to do that. They have not done it since. They were then defeated and they were out of power for four years. When they came back, they decided that maybe that was not such a good idea. I don't know why.
The fact is that in 1979 the tax expenditures-that is to say, that money which could have been collected in the form of taxes but which was not collected-amounted to $32 billion. And the deficit for that year was $14 billion. So, at that time what the government did not collect in the form of tax expenditures, loopholes, shelters, super depreciation allowances, write-offs, was twice what the deficit was for that year.
It is those kinds of policies, cumulatively, which result in the fiscal situation that we find ourselves in now. I think if the government were serious about the deficit, it would get serious about closing some of these loopholes.
Surely to God, there is no reason on earth why we have to maintain something like the business and entertainment tax loophole. Many other industrialized countries of the world have done away with this, and their economies did not shrivel up and die. Many other industrialized economies in the world have wealth taxes; their economies have not shrivelled up and died. Many other countries in the industrialized world have more progressive income tax systems than we do, and they have not shrivelled up and died; in fact, many of them are more prosperous than we are.
So, I think that the government, if it is really concerned about the deficit, should look to asking those who have, and have in abundance, to pay in abundance in order to bring down a deficit that owes its origins to their abundance in the first place.
Mr. Speaker, I see you waving your finger at me. Twenty minutes goes by very fast.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you said nothing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Somebody over there said that I did not say anything. I don't think that person was listening, Mr. Speaker, because what I have done is go over a variety of things, concrete loopholes that the Minister of Finance could have closed. The Minister of Finance is always
saying: "Come up with suggestions". We have come up with suggestions. Year after year we have made suggestions, but those suggestions are not heard. Why are they not heard? Because if those suggestions were implemented, the people who run the Conservative Party of Canada and who run this country would not be very happy. The people down at the Business Council on National Issues or at the Canadian Clubs and the Carleton Clubs and all the other clubs where decisions are made about the country, they would not be very happy. Maybe the Tories could not go down there for lunch any more. They might have to go to some cafeteria somewhere and eat with ordinary folk.
I will not believe that the Minister of Finance is serious about deficit reduction until he hits these people. Until he does, I believe that the Conservative Party is using the deficit as a political cover for doing things that they would ideologically prefer to do in the first place.
