speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the member for Winnipeg Transcona in the finance role he has now taken on. It would be wonderful if he could come to the finance committee meetings and go over tax expenditure hearings and give us some excellent advice.
The tax expenditure material is available. The finance committee did major studies on that at the time of the last major tax reform on income tax, going over every particular allowance to see what could be done to reduce any tax expenditure and I did not hear any great suggestions coming from him or his members or the member on the committee, his House leader, at that time. But perhaps he could get together with his House leader and find those various ideas.
Really, what he has said is that we should have no deficit. What we ought to do is make the rich pay. That is the kind of argument I heard once in an election from a Mandst-Leninist candidate. I was wondering if the member would like to define to this House who are the rich. How much more would he want us to increase taxes for those earning $28,000 a year, for those earning $58,000 a year? How much more would he want to put on their backs? Would he be specific? Make the rich pay. Well, who are the rich and who should pay? Give us the names, give us the people. What are the rates?

Let us not have any more of this ballyhoo, let us have the rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it amusing to have the member for Mississauga South accuse anybody else of ballyhoo, because the one thing he could have done when he got up would have been to have answered the long list of tax loopholes I pointed out that the government has not changed. But he never chose to comment as to why the government did not close them down. In the same way the Minister of Finance responding to me yesterday in the House only chose to debate me on one point and completely ignored all the rest.
It simply lacks all credibility for the member to get up and suggest somehow that I might regard people who make $28,000 a year as in the category of the rich. If the finance committee has done even a fraction of the study that the member claims, he would know just how ridiculous a claim that is.
The member knows to whom I am referring. The member knows absolutely and perfectly to whom I am referring. He knows about all the large profitable corporations in this country that pay absolutely no taxes at all on the corporate side. He knows that his own party has reduced a number of categories in the income tax system that results in a case where somebody making $60,000 a year pays the same amount as somebody making $600,000.
Perhaps the member could get up and tell us why he continues to defend real estate developers who receive all these tax credits for write-offs, for mergers and take-overs and all these sorts of things. Why is he a defender of the paper economy by which so many people have made millions by doing absolutely nothing over the last 10 or 15 years?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member has commented on how there are countries as prosperous or more than ours but nevertheless, for example, tax wealth. They tax some of their well-to-do people much higher on income tax than Canada does and yet he says those countries have not had their economies shrivel up.
The Budget
The kind of taunt that is very often tossed against the member or others who make that comment is that the wealthy people if they were taxed at all according to their ability to pay would simply run away to another country and take all their wealth with them.
I would like the hon. member to comment on the conduct of this country for the years during World War n and for two or three decades after when the tax rates were much more fair regarding people's ability to pay, how this country fared in those days and whether the wealthy people ran away from this country then.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for that question. He points out that the balance which used to exist in this country between the tax burden which was borne by the corporate sector and the tax burden which was borne by individual Canadians has disappeared. The burden on individual Canadians has risen, both in the form of incomes taxes and also in the form of consumption taxes, the latest incarnation of that being the GST, and the burden on the corporate sector has gone down, down, down, down until it has almost gone off the graph.
The question concerning whether if we were trying to reverse that, that people would leave, is interesting- that is to say rich folk would leave, because poor people generally have to stay where they are, and generally they are more dedicated to their country anyway because they have not been brought up in private schools where they learn to be dedicated to money rather than to countries or to society.
The fact of the matter is that if there are any Canadians here who think that the tax system would be enough to make them move to another country, then I have only one thing to say to them: "good-bye, good riddance, get lost, go somewhere else," because we can build a country without those kinds of people. In fact, we can build a better country without those kinds of people.
The fact of the matter is that if we were willing to enter into a long-term investment strategy to build up infrastructure in this country, technological capability, skilled worker capability and research and development, we would to create a certain kind of country that people would want to live in, work in and invest in anyway. This is what is called in a recent article in the Atlantic Monthly by Robert Reich "the virtuous cycle" rather than the "vicious cycle" which this government has got us into by trying to lower wages, not spend on infrastructure, and attract foreign investment. But when you lower wages

The Budget
and you do not spend on infrastructure, things get worse, people are not willing to invest, then you figure you have to lower wages one more time. You get into this downward spiral of degrading your own country, socially, economically and environmentally.
I would recommend to the government that it have a look at that article and consider getting out of the vicious cycle it is in now and get into what Mr. Reich has called "the virtuous cycle", which I think other countries-not the United States-but some European countries have been in for a long time, where they do not have a problem in attracting foreign investment because they have created the kind of skilled work force and technological adaptability and other forms of social benefits and strengths that make people want to invest and live there regardless of the fact that they have to pay taxes in order to create that kind of society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, forgive me for kneeling like this on my seat, but it is the best I can do in my condition.
I am happy to speak on these seventh Estimates presented by the Conservative government. What is most disheartening about the comments made on these seventh Estimates is that the Opposition is repeating the same thing every time. We have heard seven times now the same negative comments on the seven Estimates the Minister of Finance has tabled. Nevertheless, these have been gradually bringing the country back on the right track.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to review briefly the economic situation of Canada over the past ten years. But first, I would like to respond to my hon. colleague who just made reference to corporations which allegedly pay no tax among other things. That is false, Mr. Speaker, absolutely false. Since we came to power, in 1984, legislative amendments were brought forward so that Canadian corporations now pay their fair share.
Again, the hon. member provided no specific example of tax shelters for corporations in Canada. There is a good reason for that, Mr. Speaker: All tax shelters have been eliminated. There is even a tax for big corporations. Corporations have to pay taxes whether or not they make profits. Unfortunately, the hon. member failed to mention that. He failed to mention what this government has accomplished for social justice, as he failed to point out that all Canadian taxpayers, every individual, man or woman, are subject to a minimum income tax and that no one can avoid paying income tax through whatever mean or tax shelter.
Let's not forget that the taxation system established two years ago, which has reduced the tax burden of Canadians-and this is something else my friend forgot to say-; it is a system which is more equitable, fairer, a system with only three brackets, where people earning less pay less tax, and where those who earn more pay more. And that, Mr. Speaker, is something he forgot to mention.
At the beginning of my speech, I wanted to mention it to him.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to read extracts from an editorial which appeared in Le Nouvelliste, an editorial written by Mr. Claude Bruneau and entitled Beyond the Budget, the deadlock remains. Mr. Bruneau said, and I quote: "Canadians everywhere urge Mr. Wilson to achieve two aims: reduce the deficit and stimulate the economy. But at the same time, they forbid him to use two means of going about it: tax hikes and pumping new money into the system, or spending". And he went on to say: "You can't ask one to do the impossible". And further still: "And in all that has been said in the last two days, we can find no trace of the ideal budget which would solve the problem without causing a public outcry".
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these few words by Mr. Bruneau show that Canadians have come to realize how important and serious the deficit and the national debt have become.
You know, Mr. Speaker, we must not delude ourselves. When we speak of services provided to Canadians by all levels of government, federal, provincial, and municipal, as well as by the schools, we are speaking of services which have to be paid for. Canadians are starting
February 28, 1991

to realize that, in effect, when they pay their taxes, it is for these services that they do it.
The question today is this: Are we willing to spend more to keep the services we have? That is the question. This year, we have a deficit of $30 billion, and without the cuts and the extraordinary performance of our Finance Minister, we would have had a deficit of $35 billion. And we also have a national debt which, as was pointed out earlier, has doubled in she years. Mr. Speaker, 87 per cent of the increase in the national debt is due to the interest we have to pay on the debt we inherited in 1984-87 per cent! This means that although the government has reduced its annual deficit, it is still and it must keep working on reducing its annual deficit, Mr. Speaker, because this debt is not the debt of Ottawa's elected representatives it is the debt of every single Canadian. Mr. Speaker, 36 cents out of every federal tax dollar goes to paying off the interest on the debt.
Not a single family in the riding of Trois-Rivieres or in your own riding, Mr. Speaker, could survive if it had to spent 36 cents of every dollar on interest payments alone, without even paying back the capital, Mr. Speaker. No family could manage that. And we can't manage it, either. That is why these and other measures that will be taken are so severe. That is why provincial governments have a debt average of 11 cents per revenue dollar, which we could call reasonable.
Municipalities don't have the right to have a deficit. They are lucky. We, Mr. Speaker-thanks to the careless management of the previous government, which did have the right to incur a deficit, to have a national debt-had to pick up the pieces.
Mr. Speaker, in 1981-82, people were talking about a recession. This was 1981-82. The deficit was $14 billion. The government at the time doubled that amount, Mr. Speaker. The deficit soared to $28 billion in one year, the excuse being that Canadian men and women had to be helped through a difficult period. You know the results. The inflation rate was 10 per cent. Interest rates were around 22 per cent. The deficit doubled and it didn't solve a thing.
The Budget
Thking money out of the pockets of some Canadian taxpayers and trying to put it in the pockets of other Canadians is no way to deal with a recession or inflation or interest rates. They tried this in 1981-82 and it was a real flop. Mr. Speaker, our Finance Minister has brought down a straightforward budget for economic recovery. He didn't raise taxes so he didn't stimulate inflation. He didn't spend more money, so he didn't make inflation go up, and he is taking care of lowering interest rates.
This is a budget to put companies and individuals on the road to recovery. It is realistic and adapted to the present situation, Mr. Speaker. The opposition's comments are typical. They keep talking about giving away money, investing money, but the question is always: Sure, you can invest money but where do you get it? I repeat, as Mr. Bruneau pointed out so eloquently, there is no one on the opposition side, to my knowledge and his knowledge, who has found a way to raise revenue which we have left untried.
Mr. Speaker, that is the major problem we have to face. There are no draconian cutbacks in this budget. There are no major cuts that might shock Canadians. And I am glad to see there is nothing that effects the riding of Trois-Rivieres. However, Mr. Speaker, there are two extraordinary new measures. First, legislation to prevent departments from overspending their budget. And that Mr. Speaker, is news.
I think it is important, something which was positively emphasized in general. The other excellent measure is that specific legislation will be introduced to make sure that, by law, all revenues from the Goods and Services Thx will be allocated solely to bringing the public debt under control. Thanks to this excellent legislation, Canadian men and women will be assured that this government is using revenues from the GST to reduce the deficit and not to finance new spending programs which the Opposition is asking for daily, because they constantly ask us to increase spending.
When, as a young boy, I asked my father for money, sometimes he would say: "Where do you want me to get it?" Now, I am asking the Opposition where do they want the government to get the money? It is all very nice to keep on asking for money, but the time comes when the debt must be paid. The credit card is at the limit. Canadians understand now that such is our situation.

February 28, 1991
The Budget
They will talk again about the so-call cuts which the Federal government is making in the transfer payments to the provinces. There are not such cuts. There are mainly two kinds of transfer payments to the provinces, namely the established financing programs and the equalization payment programs. Minister Wilson said that as far as Established Program Financing is concerned, the amount is frozen. Freezing and cutting are two different things. That is for one program. As for the equalization payments, they continue to increase.
Which means that from one year to the next, the provinces will get more money, especially those which are getting equalization payments and which are considered less affluent. For instance, Quebec received $8.2 billion in 1984-85; it will get $10.2 billion in 1990-91. This is a large amount which accounts for 30 per cent of Quebec's budget.
The provinces all together will get $36 billion-not $36 million-per year and as the Auditor General said, the Federal government transfers to the provinces $36 billion without getting a receipt. The provinces are free to spend that money as they please.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, it is important to emphasize that because all departments here in Ottawa-the departments of my colleagues at Health and Welfare, the Secretary of State or Transport Canada-have to account for every cent they spend. And so they should. The Auditor General is responsible for checking all that, except for the $36 billion transferred to the provinces. The federal government has full confidence in the provincial administrations and let them spend that money as they see fit.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all Canadians are aware of the extent of the problem in this country. And there are other problems besides that one. You will hear other people claim that the deficit is a minor issue, that the Constitution is more important. We each have or own priorities. When the economy is in the doldrums, everything else is down. That is the message Mr. Wilson wanted to convey. First things first, all Canadians must have bread and butter on the table. So what does that call for. It calls for business people who have faith in the administration of their government. It calls for business people who are satisfied that this government can indeed administer public finances, opt for harsh measures, and have enough political courage to implement them.
Criticizing comes easy to members opposite. I have been here for six and a half years and have yet to hear an opposition member make a positive comment on any of the legislation introduced by this side of the House. Never did I hear members opposite say: Well, this is a good piece of legislation. We agree it is good. Others we feel are not good, but this one is. Never, Mr. Speaker! Not one piece of legislation ever got their approval. It is mathematically impossible for a government not to pass a good piece of legislation in six and a half years. And the best evidence in that respect-all mathematical considerations aside-is that the people-

speechtext: Nonsense!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-in 1988, the people acknowledged what we had done and we were reelected.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see we woke up someone on the other side. That is nice to see.
.
Mr. Speaker, again I must point out that this is not a cut-back but a freeze on established programs financing and an increase in equalization payments. I would suggest that the provinces-all provinces have boosted they expenditures by about 5 or 6 per cent a year since 1984 while our government has kept its yearly increases to 3 per cent-should examine their own performance. They have to look at the current situation in this country-they are part of it-and realize that if the federal government cannot afford increases over 3 per cent perhaps they too should consider imposing some restrictions.

Mr. Speaker, we were finally able to wake them up! That is a good sign.
So, Mr. Speaker, no one had the guts to say we had introduced some good pieces of legislation. This year, with this budget, and given the economic situation we are in, the opposition should support the budget and all the work that is being done to facilitate the economic recovery in Canada.

February 28, 1991

Mr. Speaker, you are telling me my time is almost up. In conclusion, I would like to read two articles, two editorials, one of which was published in La Presse yesterday, the second one, in Le Soleil. In Le Soldi, the article is entitled "Wilson sets an example". I think that title says a lot, not only to the provincial and municipal governments, but also to the business people. "Wilson sets an example".
In La Presse, Mr. Speaker, the editorial was entitled "An Honest and Far-Seeing Budget". Mr. Speaker, we often hear that a picture is worth a thousand words. In this case, I would say that these two titles are worth a thousand words.
Mr. Speaker, again, I invite the opposition to support the budget and the government in its effort to trigger Canada's economic recovery.

The Budget
Sure, the debt is causing a lot of problems, that is obvious, but the recession is giving us problems too. The budget you brought in did not provide any solutions; you made forecasts based on projections that-

You are always promising things, but meanwhile we lose many jobs; people are unhappy, our country is coming apart, we do not know where we are going.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must apologize to the hon. member because I remember I worked with her on the bill, and I remember she agreed to do that. I apologize, because I remember now.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the hon. member that since 1984, the number of individuals and families that has managed to rise above the poverty line has increased. There are fewer poor people now than there were in 1984. And that, Mr. Speaker, is something the hon. member will have to recognize as well.
As for the debt, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member brought this up but I would like to remind her that in 1984, the debt was $200 billion. Since that time, interest payments on the debt are roughly equivalent to our annual deficit. The hon. member can check this: 87 per cent of the increase in the national debt represents the interest payable on a debt that existed before I was here. I know she doesn't like to hear that, but it's the truth, Mr. Speaker. We have to live with it, she does and I do and all Canadians do.
That's the problem. That's why I say that every time her party asks or she asks for more money, it has to come from somewhere. The question is, where do we get the money we need to pay for the expenditures she wants, in whatever area? Of course, as a government, we can spend in practically every area. There are plenty of opportunities for spending. But where do we get the money? That is the question.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out to the hon. member, that when she talks about divisions across the country, last year her caucus helped to create those divisions.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Further questions? The hon. member for Edmonton East.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted that towards the conclusion of the hon. member's remarks he said-I am relying on the translation-"We need a government in which business can have confidence".
Given the indulgence, not to say the bottomless generosity, with which this government has treated its soulmates in the Business Council on National Issues, I should think that big business- big corporations and the wealthy in this country-would not only have confidence in this government, they would be enchanted with it. Anything less could only be seen by fair-minded people as the most churlish ingratitude on their parts.
February 28, 1991

However, the hon. member started his speech saying that my confrere from Winnipeg was out to lunch when he was claiming that there were people in this country who were not paying taxes.
The proof of the pudding is in the tasting. Revenue Canada produces annual statistics for which 1988 was released in November of last year. It showed that of all those Canadians earning $250,000 or more in 1988, 140 of them paid no tax. That was up by 40 per cent from the same figure for 1987. Of those earning $50,000 or more, fully 5,430 paid no tax and that was up by a whopping 87 per cent from the year earlier.
How this can be construed by anyone as evidence of a fair taxation system quite escapes me. But I would be fascinated to listen to the hon. member's attempt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I don't have offhand the figures that the hon. member mentioned. However, I hope he will understand, since he has been repeating the same thing for two years, and I hope too that the Canadian people will understand.
There is now, in the Income Thx Act, provision for a minimum personal tax, and there are only three tax reduction schemes. First, the person has suffered a loss. He or she can deduct it from his or her income, and this is only fair, if you lose money you should be able to claim the loss.
Second, the person has made charitable gifts, and third the person is paying alimony. These are the only three possibilities allowing a person earning, say $100,000, not to pay income taxes. If that person does not pay taxes it is because he or she is entitled to these deductions, and they are the only three. My colleague might not understand that, but if he had lost $50,000 last year he would be glad to be able to deduct that loss from his income. If it is a loss it can be deducted, but these are the only three reasons.
I will conclude by saying that my colleague should go back to his books and try to understand the system.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Central Nova. I am sorry; the hon. member for South West Nova.
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I had the
power of the member for Central Nova, I would do a few things differently, Mr. Speaker.
In the finance minister's budget speech this week he spoke solemnly of the need for realism and I quote:
-we must deal with the world as it is, and not as we might wish it to be.
That is the finance minister's view of the world, but he neglected to add that the uncertain world Canadians now face is largely of his making.
This, after all, is our first made-in-Canada recession, and given this government's trade and economic policies, recessions may soon be the only thing we will be able to make in Canada. It falls to the members of the Liberal opposition to set the record straight on both the extent of the government's responsibility for economic mess and how its prescription for recovery will affect average Canadians.
We have to put a human face on this government's so-called "plan for economic recovery". I think of it as a continuation of the government's plan for the end of Canada, a Canada as we used to know it.
Somebody said that The Gazette this week showed a picture of the Prime Minister with Schefferville behind with an X through it and he was holding Canada in his hand with a question mark. I have tried to trace that cartoon because I think it is very real as to what is happening in Canada.
Let us talk about the deficit. The member from Trois-Rivieres has his ideas. I commend him for his ideas, but I would also like to talk about it from the other side.
In every budget since 1984, the Minister of Finance has loudly proclaimed his unshakeable commitment to get Canada's public finances in order, to correct "the mess" he claimed the Liberal government had left for him to clean up.
In this budget he made the same claim. On page 2, he says:
We will put government finances firmly on the course to a
balanced budget.
As an aside to that, with the GST revenues he should be able to.
The time has come to call his bluff on this one. When he took over finance in 1984, the annual deficit stood at $38 billion and the accumulated public debt at $187.2 billion. This is high, to be sure, but understandable when you consider that Canada was coming out of the worst- not a made-in-Canada recession-international recession; forces that were beyond Canada since the depression.

The Budget
This, we are told, is a made-in-Canada recession, forces are in the direct control of this Minister of Finance. Nobody else can be blamed. He is the Minister of Finance. It is a made-in-Canada recession, not international, not when all the other countries in the Group of Seven had high interest rates, high inflation and high unemployment.
In 1991, the annual deficit is forecast to be $30.5 billion, and the total debt-this is the minister this week-has exploded to $388.2 billion, going to $400 billion this year. This is incredible when we remember that for most of this government's time in office, we have seen unprecedented economic growth and prosperity, and no attempt to control their deficit or to reduce the total debt.
Rather than attempt to retire the accumulated debt during the good times, this government made no progress at all. Now we find ourselves in a serious recession, a downturn that may be worse than the one in 1981-82, a made-in-Canada downturn, and the minister is saying that he has no room to manoeuvre. The minister is telling us he has no ideas; no room to stimulate the economy, no room to give Canadians some hope for the future.
Today the government is saying that we are going to have lower interest rates, lower inflation, but higher unemployment. Given the minister's poor track record in meeting his own targets in the last budget, it is unlikely that his interest rates and inflation goals will be achieved, and one has to fear that the unemployment rate will be even worse than he predicted this week.
What little progress the minister may have made toward controlling expenditure during the good times was made exclusively on the backs of the average Canadian through massive tax increases, not through any enlightenment by the minister for finding new means to create something in Canada.
Since 1984 when this government first came into power, individual Canadians have been hit with 31 major tax increases-between 1984 and 1989. Average Canadian families have suffered as much as a 176.3 per cent increase in their tax bill. The Canadian Tax Journal of
March, 1990 reports that the tax changes since 1984 have seen the average Canadian family pay about $1,000 more in tax while 640 Canadians earning more than $100,000 paid no tax at all in 1987.
Other figures show that where the 1984 tax system is still in effect, Canadians households would be paying some $11.1 billion less in taxes. That $11.1 billion could have been circulating in the economy. It could have been generating wealth and creating jobs. It could have been supporting demand for Canadian goods and services.
This year Canadians will have to put up with the goods and services tax and the additional 7 per cent burden on all their purchases. They will face this 7 per cent every day and not just when the quarterly rebate cheques come out.
I do hope that the government follows through on its plan, that it did put this 7 per cent tax in without having said why it was putting it in. But in the budget this week, the minister said he would now bring forward a new fund to show how it would reduce the accumulated debt. In the meantime, until we get that, it is going into general revenues. I do not think that is a fair expectation. The Canadian people do not want to see the government spend this money irresponsibly; not when that GST is so severe on so many Canadians.
Since 1984, during unprecedented growth and prosperity, no effort was made by the government to plug loopholes in the tax system.
I think of capital gains. Perhaps we did not need them, if you tax the working poor to the extent that they are being taxed. When speaking of capital cost allowances and inventory cost accounting, Mrs. Maxwell, when she appeared before the committee, said that those were areas that could have been closed.
Even the RRSP: Canadians were savers in the past. They used their own savings for their own direction. Maybe it is time that the RRSP should be looked at, because it certainly is not the lower income Canadians who are using the RRSP. We hope on this side that our tax group which is looking at tax reforms will look across Canada to find solutions. This government certainly does not seem to be talking to ordinary Canadians.
February 28, 1991

They should have looked at some of the program expenditures. I can mention one: ACOA, $2 billion. Where did the $2 billion go? As it now stands, ACOA is using the money to help some businesses. I don't know how some businesses get it and others don't, but that is the discretion of somebody in ACOA, creating, in my opinion, unfair business advantages. It has created an unfair playing field for many entrepreneurs, when it should be spending to upgrade the regional economy generally.
What do I mean by "upgrading"? We need to improve water and sewer services, transportation services; we need to improve skill development; we need to ensure that economic development will be environmentally sustainable. I take note, with considerable regret, that these latter two-skill development and environmental protection-have taken a serious blow in the budget. We need to develop this regionally so that the region, as a whole, can compete more effectively in the Canadian, North American and world markets.
Unless such basic infrastructure changes are made, we will continue to see ACOA-funded businesses fail, like the closing of Dominion Textiles, a textile plant that had existed for 115 years or more. So many jobs are gone just like that. They have gone to Quebec, when it started in Nova Scotia as a textile plant. We have to ask ourselves why did it go to Quebec? Why is it more effective to have a textile plant in Quebec than in Nova Scotia?
I myself think that it will not just stop in Quebec, it will go to the U.S. Under the free trade agreement that is where some of the jobs in Yarmouth have already gone.
The Atlantic Defence Industries, with several millions of dollars of both provincial and federal assistance has gone under. It has a life of six months to finish the contract.
Why this? Why the selectivity and not longer lasting? Why is ACOA not telling us what is wrong?
We will also see the tourist business go under, because we see big grants to some hotels and not to others. You can take probably any area and find that one was funded by ACOA and an existing business is not getting the funding. It is not a fair playing field.
Had the government been genuinely creative in addressing the deficit over the past few years, it might not be in the ridiculous position of trying to balance the books during a recession. It is too late to do that now. You cannot, in my opinion, balance the budget when we are in a recession. You cannot balance a budget with growing unemployment. You cannot balance a budget
The Budget
when business bankruptcies are running at record levels. You cannot balance a budget on the backs of the unemployed and the under-employed, the working poor, and those working in unstable part-time and low-paying service sectors.
Let me talk about the budget as it relates to Nova Scotia. Let's look more specifically at the effect of the budget forecasts in cuts, as it will affect my own province.
The minister forecasts an unemployment rate for 1991 of 10 per cent. This is a national average, of course. In Nova Scotia, we usually have a higher rate than the national average. In 1989, for example, the Atlantic rate was 9.9 per cent, 2.2 per cent above the national rate. When you consider the lay-offs that are hitting my area alone, in Yarmouth where 300 jobs will be lost at Dominion Textile plant, in Bridgetown where Atlantic Defence Industries may soon close-and that has only been around since the last election project; that was an election project. Atlantic Defence Industries may soon close for good, taking some 200 jobs with it and, of course, the effect of the new individual quota system on Scotia Fundy inshore fishermen and processors alone may cost one-half of existing employment. The rate is only going to increase. The rate of unemployed has to increase.
Remember that the unemployment insurance rate does not account for the many discouraged workers who have given up looking. I am looking at something in which the Canadian Labour Council states that the real unemployment rate in Canada is 14.6 per cent in December because about 738,000 Canadians have been forced either to drop out of the work force or take part-time work.
The real rate of unemployment is not what the minister is talking about. He is just talking about those who are still in the labour force survey.
No, it does not take into account the hardship facing young people, the elderly, who make up the 175,000 of Nova Scotia's 1986 population of 873,000. We understand that large numbers of people have been left out in the cold by this plan for economic recovery. No, it does not take into account many thousands of Nova Scotians. We just know that the rate in Nova Scotia, even if it stays at 10 per cent, will mean that 41,930 people in Nova Scotia who were collecting unemployment insurance last November, in 1990, when the provincial rate was 10 per cent, can look forward to another year of unemployment, thanks to this government.

The Budget
They might survive if the new unemployment insurance rules brought in by this government do not force them on to the welfare system first.
The topic of welfare leads me to discuss the extension of the freeze on Established Programs Financing transfers. I should say here that the minister through government should not reduce the deficit through Established Programs Financing cuts in 1991. The minister himself said that in 1982.
I have a quote to which I will not refer, but he was talking here in this House.
The Established Programs Financing cuts will hit Nova Scotia particularly hard since Donald Savoie said in his recent report, "Reaching Maturity for ACOA", that people in Nova Scotia earn about 15 per cent of their income through transfer payments compared to the national average of 11 per cent.
Preliminary estimates show that the extension of the freeze will cost the province another $423 million in health care and post-secondary education funds. When added to the previous established program funding cuts by this government, the extension brings the cost to Nova Scotia to upward of $1.5 billion in the fiscal year 1995-96.
What does it mean to the people of Nova Scotia? It means fewer students attending our universities and colleges because tuition fees will have to go up to pay for the cutbacks. For those students who do go, it means classes that are in the hundreds and in deteriorating facilities.
Imagine the hypocrisy of our Prime Minister loudly proclaiming his commitment to upgrading our labour force skills as he presides on the systematic dismantling of our post-secondary education system. It means hospital beds being closed and longer line-ups.
Apart from their direct effect, these cuts will have an effect on provincial budgets. They will also have an indirect effect on municipal budgets and ultimately on all the people because they will see their services being cut back by the provinces not being able to share in the 50
per cent dollars under the Canada Assistance Program and also being cut back by the Established Programs Financing freezes.
A person could talk quite at length, but I have to say that the saddest part of this budget is that it does not take into account the problems that exist in the manufacturing areas in our province. In the Atlantic economy review of 1990, in agriculture, for instance, in Nova Scotia, the total farm cash receipts in 1989 were $229.9 million. In 1990 they had decreased; $228.5 million.
In fishing the total of all groundfish-and this is a sad one- caught in 1989 was 197.5 tonnes at a return of $132 million. In 1990 the amount of fish caught was 178.7 tonnes and the value of it with a higher dollar was $138.7 million. We are not giving responsible manufacturing approaches to the regional economy of our area.
We have a Minister of Fisheries who will not talk to businesses. We have a press release, I think was put out today, by the Maritime Fishermen's Union saying, unless the province and the federal government start looking at what they are doing to the inshore fishery, unless their policies are not directed to big companies, the multinationals, we are not going to have anything left of the inshore. I quote from the Maritime Fishermen's Union: "As well, the maritime inshore ground fishery cannot survive DFO's individual boat quota system which allows large companies to buy inshore quota and fish it with larger vessels. It is only a matter of time before the inshore will lose complete access to groundfish stocks, thus eliminating inshore ground fishery."
It does not listen to people. The Liberal task force on the recession heard that this government is not listening to Canadians. If it listened, this Minister of Finance might have new and innovative ideas. He will not listen.
I say to the minister; come down and talk with the Minister of Fisheries who will not talk to Nova Scotians in the fishery. I say to him; come down and talk to the people and he will know that this is not the budget that is going to take us out of the recession.
February 28, 1991

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on an excellent speech, focusing on an issue that I think we have seen to be a hallmark of the Conservative government and that is, very simply, not listening to people.
I was interested in how my colleague focused in on her area of the country, which is something we sometimes forget. When we look at a budget, we look at budget papers, we look at averages, we look at numbers, we look at statistics and, of course, we forget about people. We see that the unemployment rate is forecast to be an average of 10 per cent. Of course, my colleague reminded us all that, indeed, in her area of the country it is very likely going to be much higher.
She invited the government to listen, but did not have an opportunity to tell the government what she heard when the Liberal task force went through her area. So, I would like to ask her if she would be kind enough to tell me and, hopefully, some members on the other side who might just listen, exactly what was heard when the people of Nova Scotia spoke.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there were probably three things that came through. The representatives of the Chamber of Commerce for Nova Scotia said that the interest rates of the government had brought on an awful lot of the problems and that they had lost control of that. They also felt that the free trade agreement, for whatever it was, was certainly taking away from the manufacturing sector and that the jobs created were certainly lower paying service industry jobs, rather than manufacturing.
I tried to point out in my speech that if you lose agriculture, if you lose fisheries, you are losing high paying manufacturing jobs. Whereas, if you are creating in the service industry, you are starting at a very minimum wage and chances are those people are not going to have full-time employment. Let us say Sheraton is going to build in New Brunswick under a lot of ACOA funding, how is it to compete with other establishments there? They can start with very low wages as well. The other thing that was heard was that they are not listening to people. The mayors said that if they would just leave it as a fair playing field then we could compete, but they are not doing that. Their policies are from one point to the other.
The Budget
The third thing, of course, being in my area, they heard from fishermen who have been involved in the fishery. They have asked for the minister to come down and he will not. I cannot understand how the Minister of Fisheries can be a Minister of Fisheries, take responsible taxpayers' money and still not go and see where the concerns are for his job. I cannot understand a Prime Minister who would have a Minister of Fisheries who has not gone in to see the inshore fishery in Nova Scotia. I just show you the Maritime Union. That is not the larger boats, but the smaller boats.
The other thing that people are hearing is that this minister talked about realism. Well, reality means that disabled persons have to live on fewer dollars a month. It means that young children are going to bed at night cold and going to school in the morning hungry. It means family breakdowns, the increase of family violence and crime, all of which impose their additional costs and have to be covered somewhere in the system.
It is the ultimate irony. It will mean a reduction in the type of social services designed to help people and families who are going to be in that situation.
I want to give one example. I had a person who came in. He had a full-time job. He was entitled to unemployment insurance. He worked part-time at K-Mart. He was married and had two very young children, one of whom was sick. He was in his mid to late 20s. His take-home pay was about $400 and he was able to supplement it-some people do not realize that you can get UI benefits to supplement your income per week- to, I think, about $600. However, he needed more than $600 for a family of four to live on, even in Nova Scotia.
I phoned welfare on his behalf. When you looked at the budget, he was entitled to $41 more a month out of such a rich country. There were no jobs. He would have liked to have gone on training, but there was no training. He would have taken anything. In a country as rich as Canada is, to see that time and time again in the three constituency offices in my riding, it begins to hit home that something is wrong.
How do the people tell this government that its policies are not working? Where do they want them to go? They do not even have money to take them out of Nova Scotia let alone train them for other jobs that they might be able to go to. You know, $600 is not much to live on for a family of four. The man wants to work and he is working part-time. If there was a full-time job he would be working. That is what people are saying.

The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been involved in the budgetary process in Parliament since 1979. I have been involved in lockups with Ministers of Finance since then.
I remember the budget of 1979, as I am sure you do, Sir, where the hon. member for St. John's East presented a budget that would have balanced. It would have provided for a tax on gasoline of 18 cents a gallon and would have given mortgage interest deductibility.
At that time in 1979, the funded debt of the country was $44 billion. I say "funded debt" because that is really the debt we should be talking about. What do we owe the bondholders? What do we owe the people from whom we borrow money on treasury bills? What do we owe people who have Canada Savings Bonds?
At the end of December 1979, we owed those people $44 billion. Then came the government that was elected in February 1980. By the end of its term, the funded debt for this country was $163 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is it today, Don?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are coming to that.
That funded debt was increased by that party in one Parliament only, four and a half years, a little better, by $119 billion.
Today on February 22, 1991-the last Bank of Canada statement on the amount of outstanding funded debt in the hands of the public-the amount we owed was $272 billion. I am rounding. That means the debt has increased in the six and a half years we have had the Minister of Finance in charge by $109 billion.
In terms of what we owe the public and not what is in the national accounts, not what we owe from one pocket of government to the other pocket of government, is $272 billion. That is an increase of $109 billion. All of
February 28, 1991

that increase is a result of compound interest because we have not, in the course of managing the country, been able, despite massive cutbacks in expenditures and despite tax increases, to get the matter turned around as well as we would like.
I will come around to the turning around as we go along, but I want to let my friend from Edmonton Southeast, who is an expert writing on finance matters but never comes to finance meetings, have some information. The amount we are going to have to borrow this year will be $21.6 billion, plus or minus whatever has to happen in the exchange fund.
I might point out to the member for Edmonton Southeast that we presently have $23 billion in the exchange fund if we converted it to Canadian dollars. It costs money to keep an exchange fund.
Perhaps we ought to be able to reduce some of that exchange fund, but we are concerned of course about the trading value of the Canadian dollar. It would be impossible to reduce the exchange fund and not increase the value of the Canadian dollar right away. A lot of that is built up by trying to keep the Canadian dollar reasonably modest in the exchange rate with the United States. We have to treat the exchange fund as an asset, but it is an asset that does cost the country some money to carry.
I do not want to underestimate the cost of the debt and the problems we face, but let us not get carried away with crazy figures saying: "You owe $400 billion and $450 billion", and so on. The facts are set out weekly, for the member for Edmonton Southeast, in the Bank of Canada statements. All he has to do is look at them. He has been around here long enough, and I am sure he gets them delivered to his office every week. Why does he not look?
We have had a problem with the cost of running the country. On average since 1985 the cost of expenditures on program has been restrained to a 3.7 per cent annual increase. That is less than the rate of inflation. Despite increases in taxes, and despite keeping costs less than the rate of inflation, we have not yet been able to get to the point where we do not have to go to the market to borrow further money.
The Budget
Hopefully, we will be able to do that, but this is not an easy matter. I want to speak, as I have spoken in the past, to this House on that matter.
We have a system that is a bit out of control. There are two things we have had to do and we must continue to do. First of all, we must look at the fiscal balance between ourselves as a federal government and the provinces and the responsibilities of the federal government and the provinces.
Second, we must eliminate the overlapping and duplication and triplication and quadruplication in some cases of government activity where the taxpayer-and there is only one taxpayer-pays bureaucrats.
Ihke Environment as an example. It pays bureaucrats in this government. It pays bureaucrats in the provincial government. It pays bureaucrats in the regional governments in Ontario. It pays bureaucrats in the municipal governments in Ontario and in every conservation authority it pays further bureaucrats, all dealing with environment, all with separate rules, all with separate ways of looking at things and all at enormous costs because they all get paid from one person. That is you and I in our taxes or you and I or our children when we borrow the money to pay them.
What we have to do is very seriously reduce and eliminate overlapping and duplication in government and very seriously priorize our claims on what we want from government, so we get our demands against the public purse reduced to the lowest amount possible.
Let me deal first of all with priorizing. A lot has been said about medicare. In the minister's speech he says that we treat medicare as a must. I think all of us and our constituents treat medicare as a must, but we have to do some priorizing. We cannot go on. The member for Winnipeg Transcona spoke about medicare and the erosion. We cannot go on the way we are going. We have to priorize.
I can just give a few examples. If one asked my constituents whether they would rather have medicare or the CBC, I bet they vote for medicare. If one asked them whether they would have medicare or the National Film Board, I will bet they vote for medicare. If one asked them whether they want medicare or VIA Rail, I will bet they vote for medicare. If one asks them whether they want medicare or the DIPP, I bet they vote for medicare. Let us have some priorization, and let us have

The Budget
some suggestions of priorization so it is not just duplication. It is the question of priorization of expenditures.
I take a look at some of the things we do, and those things we do, for example, in a field that comes before my committee, and that is the field of financial administration for the banks, trust companies and so on. A trust company in this country has to go to be disciplined by provincial inspectors and by the federal inspector. Both governments have offices of financial administration where they run their own show and they have their own separate rules and laws. All of that cost is borne not by government, but by you and I because you and I are the taxpayers for both of these governments.
I think what we have to do is realize that we have to restrain ourselves, and in the restraining process the federal government has in this budget brought that restraint directly to the attention of the provinces by cutting back, again in this budget, with some of the transfers.
My friends opposite decry that. I think it is important that we realize that the expenses for operating the Government of Ontario through 1984 to 1990 rose at an average rate of 10 per cent a year, back to back, one year after another. The cost of running all of the other provincial governments averaged across all provinces 7.2 per cent every year, back to back. The cost of this government has been 3.7 per cent. Somewhere along the line we have to get together with the provinces and reorganize the distribution of income, the distribution of responsibilities, and rationalize that because we cannot carry on as we are going in any realistic fashion.
I want to deal for a moment with the issue of unemployment insurance. That is a nasty question to talk about when we have a lot of unemployed people, particularly in a society where this year we will be paying out $17 billion in unemployment insurance, a full $4 billion more in unemployment insurance than last year as a result of severe unemployment.
One of the problems in this budget, in trying to balance things, in trying not to increase the public debt, is that the minister has found it necessary to increase unemployment insurance premiums. Let us take a look at those premiums to see whether we can really afford this program the way this program is written.
Under the minister's suggestion in the budget, the premiums are increased for individuals-that is individuals who work-to 2.8 per cent of payroll to about $28,000 a year. For companies which employ people, that is everybody they employ, 3.92 per cent of payroll to about $28,000 a year. That is a total of 6.72 per cent of payroll as a payroll burden. Think about it: a 6.72 per cent payroll burden represents three weeks' holiday pay for every single working person in Canada.
Do you really think your constituents would willingly give up three weeks' holiday pay for unemployment insurance premiums? These are the things that we as a Parliament have to look at. These are the costs that we have to take into account when we say to taxpayers that they have to pay for this fund or they have to pay for that fund, or we are going to have to increase their Canada pension contributions.
These costs are being borne by our constituents and these costs injure the productivity of the country because they make it more expensive to employ people. They make it necessary for companies to pass their wage costs on in their prices. They make us uncompetitive, or less competitive, than we should be in world markets.
What we have to do as a country is become more competitive. What we have to do is take a look at all of these things and ask: can we really go along with what has been happening year after year with no real change, or should we again take a look at the programs and say: "You know, we have got to change that program?"
We have got to get along with a little less benefit. We have got to get along with different criteria. We cannot just sit back and say that every program of government is all of a sudden a sacred trust and nothing can be altered, because there is only one person who we have as a constituent-and that is you and I and our friends, our neighbours and our constituents who pay taxes-the taxpayer. That person can only bear so much.
I think it is in our obligation not to just decry the problems of the budget, not just to decry the fact that taxes are going up, not just to decry the fact that programs are cut back, but to come at the cost of government by giving that cost of government a rethink.
February 28, 1991

I want to say how impressed I am with the minister's ability to cut back bit by bit on the borrowing requirements. This year the minister will require about $21.6 billion to borrow on the marketplace, depending on how the exchange fund works. Next year the minister's budget calls for $14 billion in borrowing, the following year $5 billion in borrowing, and it puts us in the position where we start paying back the national debt in 1994-95.
Compare that deficit situation with what we inherited. When we took power in 1984 the deficit was 8.6 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product. This year the United States will have a deficit of 5.7 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product and our percentage of debt to Gross Domestic Product, expressed the way they express it, expressed on a national accounts basis, is 3.5 per cent.
In other words, we have reduced the shortfall from 8.6 per cent of Gross Domestic Product to 3.5 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, and bit by bit we are turning it around.
But we cannot go on the way we are. We cannot go on with income taxes because of the inflation, partial deindexing rising year after year. Families cannot go on with the payments they are asked to make on income tax, on goods and services tax. My friends on the left call for capital taxes. We cannot go on this way and build a competitive society.
What we have to do, therefore, is learn how to train our demands on the state to what we really can afford, what we really need, not what we would like or what would be jam. Let us get our costs and our demands on government back to a more realistic level.
Our problem is very simple. For a number of years we were trained by government that any time you needed something you went to the government in prayer. You went to the government in prayer. You said: "Mr. Government, I have a problem. I want to start a business. Give me a grant. I have a problem. I need an assistance program." I need this, I need that. Give me, give me, give me. Thke it to the Lord in prayer. And what we did is we got used to receiving $1.1 for every dollar paid in taxes.

speechtext:

But everybody forgets about the taxpayer.

So I would like to know what he thinks, Mr. Speaker, because we see, year after year, that the Minister's projections are wrong. In 1985, he said that the deficit would be about $19 billion this year; we still have a $30 billion deficit. So we do not need his projections because we know that they never materialize.
I have another question. Earlier, my colleague said that he was very concerned about the debt service, and therefore about the debt itself. I would like to remind him that the total debt accumulated in 177 years since Confederation was doubled by his government in the last six years. It is something that has to be said, Mr. Speaker.
But I would like to ask him a question. If they really want to reduce the debt, they must not do it by making cuts in the programs designed to help needy Canadians. How come-read the estimates tabled today-how come the government is spending $3 billion a year on advertizing, consultations and public relations? If we are in a recession, instead of making cuts in programs for people

February 28, 1991
The Budget
who need a hospital bed or for people who need affordable housing, a roof over their head, or for people who need jobs, why not cut in government's expenses on consultation, advertizing and public relations it does not need in any case?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite obviously my friend has not been paying any attention. Let me give him some information for his record. He will note that this is the only Minister of Finance that has ever come anywhere close to being accurate with respect to his forecasts on borrowing requirements and his forecasts on public accounts debt.
On the public account debt he forecast $28.6 billion last year. He came in at $30.5 billion, but he made a change in forecast part way through the year as a result of interest rates. If he goes back to the prior year, he will find that the minister was able to come in $.5 billion less than he forecast.
On borrowing requirements, the minister forecast to borrow $21.5 billion and he had to borrow $23.5 billion. But this is the only Minister of Finance and the only government that did not do what the last government did, and that is have two borrowing authority bills a year. In one case it had three borrowing authority bills because they could not get they act together. They kept spending more money than they even forecast themselves, so they had to come back to the House time after time for more borrowing authority.
My friend from Edmonton knows that. He was there at the time. He remembers the extensive debates on borrowing authority. Perhaps he would like to tell us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member, knowing that he is and has been known to be very frank and very truthful. Having sat on the finance committee with him and knowing that he is the author of the term "gouge and screw" tax, I know he will give me a level answer. I want to know on behalf of members of
Parliament and the people of Canada something about the debt servicing reduction fund.
If we look at page 13 of the minister's budget speech, he states:
As part of our Plan for Economic Recovery, we will ensure that all GST revenues are allocated solely to the effort to bring the public debt under control.
Then if we turn to page 78 of the budget and we look at the second paragraph it says:
The Prime Minister has given a commitment that any above-projected revenues from the GST will make a contribution to deficit reduction rather than provide the leeway for an expansion in discretionary government spending.
The next paragraph goes on to say:
The fund will be established to a specified purpose account to which will be credited net GST revenues and from which will be debited public debt charges.
The attitude that seems to be given is the one that all GST revenues after the administration charges, in other words approximately $16.5 billion, will go into this specified fund and will pay down the debt at that rate per year.
My question to the member is: Can he tell us openly and honestly, as he has with the "gouge and screw" tax, the definition of "all" or the definition of "net revenues", so the people of Canada and I, in fact, will know the amount being paid into this fund?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am delighted. That is a sensible question.
The goods and services tax is a gross tax that has certain rebates to it. In particular, hospitals, schools, charities and so on receive part of their tax back. You take the gross of the tax, and those people who receive part back and that comes off the receipt of the tax.
The same applies with respect to real estate. We have a tax of 7 per cent on the transfer of a house, but if you buy a new house as a single family owner you only pay a
4.5	per cent rate, so that really there is a rebate of 2.5 per cent of the tax.
Those rebates come off the gross tax. Also coming off the gross tax is the refund to low income people that is paid quarterly. That brings it to the net tax. That is the amount of net tax that goes in the deficit reduction fund. There is no other deduction from that.
February 28, 1991

This is an honest and straightforward way of saying to the people of Canada: "We know you didn't like this goods and services tax, but we are putting it toward the debt and that is where it belongs. When we get rid of the debt maybe we can get rid of the tax".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of interesting questions to ask the hon. member opposite. He talked about unemployment insurance and how we should carry our fair share of that particular burden.
The Mayor of Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories said: "Increased unemployment insurance contributions will cost $154 a year for each worker for the city of Yellowknife. It means $35,000 to $40,000 increase in employer contributions". She goes on to say: "What may be saved at the federal level and avoided at the territorial level, will eventually be passed on to the ratepayers and municipalities. Needed infrastructure may not go ahead unless municipalities and municipal governments pay for it by raising mill rates".
With regard to the north, there is 60 to 90 per cent unemployment. The Canadian Jobs Strategy cut of $100 million is going to have an impact because unemployment is so high. Essentially unemployment insurance and training programs are like a sub-economy. I know the minister to have had an attitude toward specific groups who he feels get free stuff. He had this validated and verified in a survey that he did.
I would like to know what initiatives he would use to kick-start the economy in the north, rather than gouging and screwing the constituents of the north.

February 28, 1991

The rules are clear and unambiguous. Members are required to remain here until the vote has been completed and the count has been released.
Even this hon. member should understand the consequences of the waiver of the rule, and it is that immediately after each one of us has voted, we could very well have left. You could imagine the spectacle that that would represent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
There is a convention in this House, and it is under Beauchesne's citation 223(3):
If a Member who has heard the question put should inadvertently vote contrary to his intention, he may not be allowed to correct the mistake; but his vote must remain as first recorded. Debates, July 1, 1926, p. 5311.
Shall we carry on with debate? The hon. member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso has the floor.
A point of order, the hon. member for York South- Weston.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the point put before you for consideration was the fact that an hon. member of this House left before the vote was announced. By not removing that particular member's vote from the official record, in effect, Sir, you would be setting a precedent. That precedent would be that once you stand and your vote is recorded, you could vacate or leave the House. That is not the convention of this House. In the seven years that I have been here, it has been very clear that in order for your vote to be counted, it is essential that you remain in your seat until the vote is announced. By allowing this particular incident to carry on, as I indicated, the precedent would be set whereby throughout the course of a vote you would see members standing and then leaving the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will go to Beauchesne's Citation 223(2):
A Member must be in his own seat should he wish to vote and should remain in his seat until the division is complete and the result announced. Journals, April 18, 1956 -
There is convention here that members should remain in their seat, but it has not been done here in the last six years that I can recall. New members have come into this Chamber. I will listen to the hon. member's point of order, but there has to be a little more decorum so the
The Budget
Chair can see what is going on too. It is pretty hard to see if members walk in and out getting their drink of water while the vote is going on, and that has happened here in the last six or seven years that I can remember.
I think that we should just leave it at that. I will check and see if we can find out if this has happened. The hon. member is an honourable member. If he feels that he should come in after he has taken his trip back home, if he has caught his plane, and if he feels that his vote should be withdrawn, he will stand up in the House like any honourable member and do what has to be done. Otherwise, I think we should carry on with debate. We had another 26 minutes left. We only have about another 17 minutes left in debate.
The hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair has another point of order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that I have no alternative, as I am sure my colleagues have no alternative, but to express considerable concern about the manner of the ruling.
The Speaker, in the first instance, ruled on an issue that was not at all raised, and then the Speaker read from the rules of order to find that if in fact the hon. member did absent himself before the release of the count he had abrogated those rules. His colleague, sitting right next to him, concurred with the hon. member behind me in respect to his having left before the vote was completed.
It seems to me that it would have to be self-evident to the Speaker that if his ruling was to form the pattern of behaviour in this House, the House would be reduced to absurdity. I would ask the Speaker to change his ruling with some thought behind it.
