speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is nice to see so many government members have waited for this speech. I want to address as an Atlantic Canadian some of the serious issues touched upon by Tuesday's budget.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know that they are trying to reflect on the Hill Times, but I know the hon. member has a very serious speech and I wish he could get to it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know they are jealous, Mr. Speaker. I would like to recommence my speech. I hope I will be able to complete it before the time is up.
I want to address as an Atlantic Canadian some of the serious issues touched upon by Tuesday's budget. These are issues which go to the heart of Confederation and Atlantic Canada's place in it.
Recently, with some of my colleagues, I had the opportunity to travel throughout Atlantic Canada to see first-hand the effects of the recent recession on people in Atlantic Canada. During this time I heard the views and concerns of Atlantic Canadians about the impact of this recession, the government response to it, and what impact that is having on their lives.
In Yarmouth we listened to Bob Anthony, the warden of Yarmouth County and a small businessperson. He told us of the crushing burden of high taxes and interest rates on small businesses hi his region.
In Saint John we heard Allan Kurtz of the St. Stephen Retailers Association describe how his community, along the border with Maine, was being turned into a ghost town because of cross-border shopping since the free trade agreement came into effect.
In Harbour Grace and in Comer Brook, we were told repeatedly how federal mismanagement was killing the Newfoundland fishery and how nothing was being done to create a new and better future for Newfoundlanders.
I learned above all else that hundreds of communities in Atlantic Canada are suffering under the economic policies of this government. I cannot shake the sinking feeling that this government simply does not care.
In November 1984 the finance minister presented Canadians with an agenda for economic renewal. Now, seven years later, he presents us with a plan for economic recovery. What does Canada have to recover from? It is the consequences of the misguided and failed policies of this Tory government; that is what.
Real interest rates, which have never been so out of line with those of the United States, are throttling our businesses and are a daily reminder to investors of the economic uncertainty into which this government has plunged Canada; an unacceptably high dollar which is crippling our exporters; a trade agreement which is leading to the deindustrialization of this country and forcing Canadians to downgrade their social programs to the level of those in the United States.
Now we are presented with the Minister of Finance's seventh budget and, God willing, his last.
I firmly believe that once Canadians have had a chance to comprehend fully what this document is attempting to do, what this government is attempting to do with this budget, they will understand the devastating implications of the Conservative agenda now laid bare for everyone to see.
Let us examine the facts. In 1984 when this government came to power it promised economic renewal. It promised to reduce the deficit and to curb the growth of the debt. Above all else, it promised jobs, jobs, jobs.
What have the government's economic policies brought us? They have brought us our first made-in-Ca-nada recession, where interest rates have been pushed up past the breaking point for many Canadians; where today nearly 1.5 million Canadians are out of work;
February 28, 1991

where inflation is growing, not diminishing; where 34 consecutive tax increases by this government have foisted the tax burden squarely on the backs of lower and middle income Canadians.
The Minister of Finance now expects Canadians to believe him, that he has a firm grasp on what must be done and that Canadians should trust him and they should hang on just a little longer. I ask the minister: Why should Canadians believe him now? Why should we believe his deficit projections which have been so consistently wrong? Why should we believe his interest rate predictions which were so out of line in last year's budget? Why should we believe his Pollyanna promise of 2 per cent inflation in three years? His policies and especially the GST have actually increased inflation.
What the minister fails to make clear, what he fails to mention in his budget document, is that the consequence of trying to achieve these inflation targets will be unacceptably high unemployment.
We are now expected to believe that the Minister of Finance who got Canadians into this mess can get us out with this hocus-pocus plan for economic recovery. That is like asking Saddam Hussein to supervise the rebuilding of Kuwait.
His projections for the deficit this year stand at $30.5 billion. After several straight years of economic growth in the Canadian economy, is this the best he has been able to accomplish? How long are Canadians expected to hang on? Many Canadians are past the point of hanging on. Far too many have seen their jobs disappear. Far too many are fighting a losing battle in simply trying to keep their families sheltered and clothed and their children properly fed.
These Canadians have been ignored by the minister in this budget and, by ignoring them, the minister is punishing them, punishing them for being at the wrong end of the economic spectrum.
As members of Parliament we have often been accused of being cut off from the realities of day-to-day life in Canada. We have been accused of being insensitive to the needs of ordinary Canadians.
The Budget
Some people ask: How can we understand the plight of a man in his fifties who without warning has lost his job and is unable to get adequate retraining as he watches his unemployment insurance benefits run out? How can we appreciate what it means for a single mother to be forced to line up at a food bank, for a young person to come to the realization that he or she cannot afford to attend university, for or a fisherman to have to sell his livelihood and that of his father and his father's father because he is being squeezed out by bigger and more competitive companies?
Maybe we cannot fully comprehend what these things mean to the people directly affected, but that does not mean that we should stop caring. That does not mean that we can fool ourselves into thinking that with brave projections as to likely economic trends, we will ultimately be helping these people. Economic indicators mean little to those who are desperately looking for work.
In Canada, people need help today, right now. This government has forgotten about them or has chosen to ignore them. They point to the pages of The Financial Post or The Globe and Mail and claim their actions are justified. No one is more guilty of this than the Minister of Finance.
I truly wish the minister had joined my colleagues and me in early February when we toured Atlantic Canada, asking ordinary Canadians what could be done to reverse the tide of economic woes which had befallen our country. I wish the minister had experienced the frustration these people are feeling and the desperate sense they have that their country is falling apart.
Again and again, the same issues were raised: aging infrastructure and the unwillingness of the government to address the problem. Excessive taxation which has left Atlantic Canadians with less money and less earning power, the gross mismanagement of the fisheries which has left fishermen and fish processors crippled, and a level of unemployment which some believe the government will never address.
Nowhere I believe are these feelings more passionately felt that in my riding of Cape Breton Highlands-Can-so. Unemployment in Cape Breton is now over 17 per cent. Cutbacks in job training and increased UI premiums have left Cape Bretoners feeling that the problem is only going to get worse, because they feel this government does not care.

February 28, 1991
The Budget
What else are they to think? Last January the government cut VIA Rail passenger service from Truro to Sydney, and repeatedly CN has sought to downgrade portions of its service on the island. The application to partially close the swing bridge at the Barra Strait is yet another example.
In December this government closed the CBC station in Sydney and ended one of the most popular CBC programs in Atlantic Canada, Land and Sea.
This government has refused to support the request by Scotia Synfuels for assistance to establish a coal liquefaction plant at the Strait of Canso, which would use Cape Breton coal in an environmentally friendly way.
Indeed the minister of industry refuses to meet with the principals of this important project which has the support of community and business leaders across the island. Decreased transfer payments have jeopardized the ability of my riding's most famous institution, St. Francis Xavier University in Antigonish, to provide a quality education to its students.
It currently faces an $800,000 operating deficit, which is forcing it to reconsider many of the programs currently being offered. What makes this all the more ironic is that St. FX is the Alma Mater of the Prime Minister himself, the self-styled education Prime Minister who has claimed on the one hand that education and skills training are vital to Canada's ability to compete internationally. Then, on the other hand, he has allowed his Minister of Finance once again to continue the freeze on transfer payments, crippling our universities and forcing drastic cuts in job training programs.
My constituents need take no lessons from this government about the impact the recession is having on our economy. My constituents understand what this latest budget is about. It is about more unemployment, more cutbacks, more essential services lost, and more economic desperation. All this in the part of the country that has already seen more than its fair share. I say this knowing full well that what is true for Cape Breton Island is also true for much of Atlantic Canada.
What is most disturbing about this budget from an Atlantic Canadian perspective is what it does not do. It provides essentially no hope for the people who are feeling the brunt of the recession.
Rather than provide for additional retraining funds for the unemployed, the government has cut $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy program. Instead of encouraging businesses to hire and train unemployed workers, this budget increases unemployment insurance premiums by nearly 25 per cent. These higher UI premiums are a direct tax on jobs, a new tax on lower and middle income workers and on the businesses across the country.
This is a new tax being levied right in the middle of a recession, on the heels of the government's most massive and complicated new tax grab, the GST. It is yet another tax which will force additional businesses to lay off workers and drive others closer to the brink of bankruptcy. So much for Tory economic logic. So much for Tory compassion.
Farmers will receive $1.3 billion in this budget. That is something, but for fishermen in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere still facing a crisis in their industry there is nothing. How should the fishermen feel, Mr. Speaker? I will tell you how they feel. They feel forgotten, ignored and betrayed.
Fishermen understand what recession is all about. They also know what it is to be cast adrift by a government that has simply stopped caring about what happens to them.
In talking to fishermen over the last couple of days, one question has been asked of me over and over again: Who is supposed to represent us in cabinet? Why, when we are facing a crisis at least as serious as the one facing farmers, are we being ignored?
The answer is simple. The current minister of fisheries has simply grown tired of dealing with fishermen and representing their concerns. He does not care any more. In fact, the same minister was recently quoted as saying that he wants to spend less time dealing with the crisis in the fisheries and spend more time dealing with the issue of national unity.


February 28, 1991

That is a fine thought. If this minister does for national unity what he has done to the fisheries, then we may as well all pack up and go home right now.
